articles.title_orig: Katie Zacharia did not pass the bar exam, senior administration official says
articles.title_zh: Katie Zacharia did not pass the bar exam, senior administration official says
articles.content_orig:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam when she took it after she graduated from law school, according to a senior administration official.
The official argued that Zacharia could technically be considered a “lawyer,” though not an attorney. President Donald Trump referred to Zacharia as an “attorney” in his Truth Social post last week announcing he was tapping her as press secretary.
But several lawyers told NBC News that “lawyer” is widely understood to refer to someone who has passed the bar exam and is licensed to practice law.
Zacharia’s failure to pass the bar exam was first reported by The Wall Street Journal . Zacharia, who has repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer, faces questions about her legal credentials as the White House has not said whether she passed the bar exam.
NBC News has not found evidence that she is licensed to practice law in any state. Zacharia, who graduated from Pepperdine Law, has said she practiced law in China. Legal experts told NBC News that only Chinese citizens can sit for the Chinese bar exam. One expert told NBC News that Zacharia could have consulted on cross-border legal issues.
The D.C. Bar did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether Zacharia could be considered a “lawyer.” Zacharia lived in California but said she would move to Washington, D.C., for her new job.
The New York Times previously reported that Zacharia said in an interview Wednesday night that before she began appearing in cable news interviews, she discussed with Pepperdine’s president how to identify herself. Zacharia told the Times that she was told it was OK to use “lawyer” but not “attorney” or “esquire.” Pepperdine did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In an interview Thursday with the conservative news outlet Real America’s Voice, Zacharia said she “consulted for a very long time many people in the field, is it okay and acceptable if I label myself lawyer, not attorney at law, not Katie Zacharia esquire, but lawyer, and provide legal analysis, not legal advice.”
The answer, she added, was “absolutely, across the board.”
Zacharia denied that she misrepresented her legal qualifications, saying, “I was very careful how I executed this and I never came across as someone who was an attorney at law.”
On Wednesday, representatives from the Democracy Defenders Fund, which frequently opposes the Trump administration, asked California Attorney General Rob Bonta and George Cardona, the chief trial attorney for the State Bar of California, to investigate whether Zacharia “engaged in the unauthorized practice of law.” Cardona’s office investigates potential lawyer misconduct.
“Falsely holding oneself out as a lawyer is a criminal offense, punishable by fine or incarceration of up to a year in jail,” the letter said.
The signers included Norm Eisen, co-founder of the Democracy Defenders Fund, as well as Richard Painter, who was President George W. Bush’s ethics lawyer. Painter, now a law professor at the University of Minnesota, has been a critic of Trump. Painter does not work at the Democracy Defenders Fund.
The California attorney general’s office referred NBC News to the state bar for comment.
A spokesperson for the State Bar of California said in a statement Thursday that because of “confidentiality laws,” it could disclose only whether people passed the bar exam, not whether they sat for it.
The spokesperson said in an earlier statement that Zacharia never “appeared on a California bar exam pass list.”
The spokesperson said Thursday that the bar could not weigh in on “hypotheticals involving conduct that might be the subject of action by the State Bar.”
“As a general matter, however, California Business and Professions Code section 6126 makes it unlawful for anyone who is not an active licensee of the State Bar, or otherwise authorized pursuant to statute or court rule to practice law in California, to advertise or hold themselves out as practicing or entitled to practice law in California,” the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson told NBC News on Wednesday that the bar “cannot confirm whether it has received any complaint or is conducting any investigation,” citing confidentiality requirements.
Reached for comment, the White House referred to a post from White House communications director Steven Cheung, who criticized a different group that asked the State Bar of California to investigate Zacharia. In that post , Cheung referred to the watchdog group Campaign for Accountability as “a radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome.”
Cheung also said in a statement that Zacharia “is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team.”
“She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary,” he said.
The White House also referred to a previous statement from Zacharia in which she said she “practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials.”
The spokesperson for the State Bar of California told NBC News on Tuesday that the state does not have records of Zacharia’s having been licensed to practice law in the state.
Gabe Gutierrez is a senior White House correspondent for NBC News.
Monica Alba is a White House correspondent for NBC News.
Megan Brand is a politics reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: MAGA World Is Counting on a Bolsonaro Win in Brazil
articles.title_zh: MAGA World Is Counting on a Bolsonaro Win in Brazil
articles.content_orig:
Argentina's President Javier Milei and Eduardo Bolsonaro at the Hispanic Heritage Gala in Washington, DC. Alex Wroblewski /AFP/Getty
On Wednesday evening, conservative businesspeople, digital influencers, and US government officials flocked to the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, DC, for the Latino Wall Street-organized inaugural Hispanic Heritage Gala. The event’s guest of honor was Javier Milei, the far-right president of Argentina, who has been described as “Trump’s doppelgänger” and a “ proxy ” for the US leader in Latin America. But that evening, all eyes were on another politician: Eduardo Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and brother of  presidential contender Flávio Bolsonaro.
Attendees in sparkly gowns and tuxedos swarmed to Eduardo for selfies and handshakes. Many asked after his 71-year-old father, whose health issues have allowed him to serve a 27-year sentence for attempted coup at home. Others gushed over his brother Flávio Bolsonaro’s lead in the first round of a close presidential race against incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. He talked to MAGA media (including the boxer-turned-LindellTV White House correspondent Cara Castronuova) and posed alongside Javier Negre, a controversial Spanish communicator dubbed the “King Midas of virality” for right-wing propaganda . At one point, a woman approached to pray with him for Brazil.
Eduardo is more than a cheerleader for his would-be presidential sibling; he is poised to become the next foreign minister of Brazil in a potential Flávio Bolsonaro government. Since moving to the United States in early 2025, the younger Bolsonaro has lost his congressional seat for missing more than 80 percent of sessions and a job as a federal police investigator for “abandoning his post.” Last week, Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes issued a warrant for his arrest after he was sentenced to more than four years in prison for trying to interfere with his father’s criminal case by lobbying the Trump administration. But in the MAGA world, Eduardo is a star—and his brother’s ascent to power is a fait accompli.
“We’re going to kick out the communist dictator in Brazil, and we’ll paint the continent blue,” Milei roared after warmly hugging Eduardo, who threw kicks in the air. Conservatives, he said, “cannot give an inch in our reconquest of the hemisphere.” Eduardo cautioned that the election results weren’t final yet, but the tone was openly celebratory. “When we confirm the victory of my brother Senator Flávio Bolsonaro as president of Brazil,” he said in a speech that followed Milei’s, “we’re going to achieve a new, what I call, the Golden Era of Latin America.”
The optimism in the room wasn’t unjustified. Flávio came out ahead of Lula following the first round of voting, albeit by a small margin, and the election of conservative candidates to Congress all but guarantees that the legislature will move further to the right. The presidential race will be decided in a runoff on October 25. A Bolsonaro win would bring Brazil—Latin America’s largest economy and a coveted prize for its wealth of rare earths —back into the fold of populist right-wing leaders ideologically aligned with Trump, sealing the “ orange wave ” that has swept a region the American president sees as his sphere of influence. “We have everything to be just like the US,” Eduardo said.
The former lawmaker has used his ties to Trump’s circle to court the White House to impose tariffs on Brazil and sanctions on judicial authorities like Moraes while making the case for his father’s freedom. Trump heeded the call, linking a 50 percent tariff on Brazilian goods announced last year to a “ witch hunt ” trial against Jair Bolsonaro and accusing Brazil’s government officials of “persecuting” the former president. In May, a couple of days after Eduardo and Flávio Bolsonaro met with Trump, the US government designated two criminal groups active in Brazil as terrorist organizations.
If Flávio Bolsonaro’s victory materializes, Brazil is expected to join the Shield of the Americas coalition. Despite his alleged connections to militia groups in Rio de Janeiro, Flávio has positioned himself as a tough-on-crime candidate, invoking the brutal regime of Nayib Bukele in El Salvador as an example to be followed. Flávio and Eduardo have visited CECOT, the mega prison where migrants sent by the Trump administration reported being tortured. At the gala, Eduardo name-checked Bukele and praised Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella, who calls himself “El Tigre,” for posing in front of body bags.
“Everybody who gives a hard time to the criminals, we love,” he remarked, adding that “for the first time we’re going to see all the countries [in Latin America] fighting narcoterrorism.” The audience approved. One real estate entrepreneur who does business in Honduras told me he found the speech “inspirational” and that Brazil should implement the “Bukele model.” As speakers on stage talked about getting rid of crime and defeating socialism, guests who paid between $3,000 and $10,000 to be there enjoyed wagyu meatballs, smoked duck with blackberries, grilled stuffed avocado, and smoked beef tenderloin. “The best is yet to come,” Eduardo declared, vowing to free Brazil, starting with his father.
The Brazilian elections have raised the specter of outside influence, with the country’s intelligence agency warning of risk of US interference in light of the Trump administration’s priority of reaffirming its hegemony in Latin America. Earlier this year, the Brazilian government denied visas to two senior State Department officials whose visit was intended to cast doubt on Brazil’s voting system ahead of the election. Several Democrats have accused the Trump administration of “acting as an agent of interference and destabilization,” citing a “troubling pattern of interference” in electoral processes in Argentina, Honduras, and Colombia. Trump, experts have observed , is playing “kingmaker” in the region. (The event’s organizers lamented that Trump couldn’t be there because he was in Alaska campaigning ahead of the midterms. But after several minutes of audio issues, they showed a recorded message from the president urging US voters to “pretend” he’s on the ballot and get out to vote.)
Speaking to reporters before the gala, Eduardo dismissed concerns that the United States is meddling in Brazil’s elections, repeating unfounded claims that, during the Biden administration, USAID funded NGOs and the media to prevent the re-election of Jair Bolsonaro in 2022 under the guise of fighting disinformation.
“Brazil has already suffered international interference,” he said. “What I see now is the opposite.” First order of business would be to “purge this cancer called Alexandre de Moraes from the Supreme Court,” Eduardo said, calling the justice a “tyrant.” Otherwise, he added, his brother wouldn’t be able to govern. When asked if he had plans to return to Brazil, he said he wouldn’t want to go to jail, “being innocent.”
Eduardo moved around the ballroom shadowed by far-right blogger Allan dos Santos, a close Bolsonaro ally and self-described “most persecuted journalist in the world.” Dos Santos, who lives in the United States, is considered a fugitive from Brazilian justice in the context of probes into the dissemination of fake news and creation of digital militias. A fixture of US conservative events, Eduardo rubbed elbows with an Italian influencer who supports Germany’s far-right AfD party and schmoozed with CPAC chair Matt Schlapp and his wife Mercedes. She gave the Bolsonaros a shoutout in her speech, predicting Flávio would be elected president of Brazil. “We got Latin America back on track,” she said.
Toward the end of the evening, as guests danced to La Bamba, Conga, and the Macarena, I chatted with Lena Ruseva, who wore a long red dress with Trump’s face on it and the words “drill, baby, drill.” Calling herself an “America

articles.title_orig: Julie Taymor and Elliot Goldenthal’s new musical sets New York world premiere
articles.title_zh: Julie Taymor and Elliot Goldenthal’s new musical sets New York world premiere
articles.content_orig:
Titled “The Grand Delusion,” the new musical will play at BAM in spring 2027.
A new musical by two-time Tony Award winner and Oscar nominee Julie Taymor and Oscar winner and Tony nominee Elliot Goldenthal, will have its world premiere at Brooklyn Academy of Music (BAM) in 2027. Titled “The Grand Delusion,” the musical will run at BAM’s Harvey Theater from May 11 through June 6.
Set in modern-day New York City, India and a metaphysical plane, “The Grand Delusion” is described as a “transporting and erotic musical fantasy.” The new musical combines dance, immersive design, puppetry and music.
The new musical is being produced by special arrangement with Chunsoo Shin and OD Company, the producer of Broadway’s “The Great Gatsby.” Shin also earned Tony nominations as a co-producer of “Titaníque” and the 2012 revival of “Jesus Christ Superstar.”
Taymor and Goldenthal are longtime partners and collaborators. They co-wrote the book for the 1996 Broadway musical “Juan Darién,” which Taymor directed and for which Goldenthal penned the music and lyrics. “Juan Darién” was nominated for five Tonys, including Best Musical, Best Direction of a Musical for Taymor and Best Original Musical Score for Goldenthal. In 2000, “The Green Bird,” directed by Taymor and with music by Goldenthal, bowed on Broadway. In Broadway circles, Taymor is best known for her Tony-winning direction and costume design of Disney’s “The Lion King.” Beyond the Main Stem, Taymor and Goldenthal  collaborated on the opera “Grendel,” which was named a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for Music in 2007, and the 2017 Broadway revival of “M. Butterfly,” for which Goldenthal wrote original music and Taymor directed. Goldenthal also composed the Academy Award-winning score for the 2002 Frida Kahlo biopic “Frida”; the pair were nominated for Best Original Song for “Burn It Blue” from the movie.
“The Grand Delusion” will mark the duo’s first major theatrical collaboration in years.

articles.title_orig: Congo Ebola outbreak spreads to new province bordering Central African Republic
articles.title_zh: Congo Ebola outbreak spreads to new province bordering Central African Republic
articles.content_orig:
This article is part of a developing story.
Nearly 1 in 4 confirmed Ebola patients in North Kivu is a child under the age of 5, yet children continue to face major barriers to accessing innovative medical tools.
Daniella, 10, smiles at the camera after being discharged from the Munigi Ebola treatment center. | DR Congo 2026 © Miora Rabearisoa/MSF
Children are paying a devastating price in the Ebola outbreak unfolding in northeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). They account for a significant share of confirmed Ebola disease cases and are also more likely to die from the disease than adults.
According to Epicentre, the Doctors Without Borders/Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) epidemiological research center, nearly 1 in 4 confirmed Ebola cases in North Kivu province is a child under 5. MSF is deeply concerned by the disproportionate impact on children and is calling for the medical and research response to ensure that they are no longer left behind in access to vaccines, treatments, and clinical research.
The impact on children is particularly stark In North Kivu, where 24 percent of confirmed cases are among children under 5 years old; more than half on them — 54 percent — are infants under 1. In Ituri, by comparison, children under 5 account for 13 percent of confirmed cases, of whom 46 percent are under 1 year old.
While Ebola remains a deadly disease for all age groups, the youngest children face the highest risk of death. At the Ebola treatment center in Butembo, North Kivu, MSF teams have recorded a particularly high fatality rate among children. Between June and September 2026, 24 out of 30 children admitted to the center died from Ebola disease — most of whom were under the age of 5. The rapid spread of the disease in communities and limited access to specialized care in health facilities are contributing to these alarmingly high fatality rates.
A child-centered approach must be at the heart of medical care, operational planning, and research efforts.
“Primary health facilities often lack the specialized expertise, equipment, and infection prevention and control measures needed to identify and safely manage suspected cases,” explains Stéphanie Hoffmann, project coordinator for MSF in Butembo. “Most of the [children] admitted to our Ebola treatment center in Butembo had already been hospitalized for other illnesses in several facilities during the days or weeks before their admission. Their family members did not have Ebola themselves, and it is highly likely that these children contracted the disease inside health care facilities.”
To maintain access to essential non-Ebola health services while reducing the risk of Ebola transmission in health care facilities, infection prevention and control measures must be urgently strengthened in health facilities. This includes ensuring the availability of personal protective equipment (PPE) and strengthening training for health care workers in non-Ebola health centers across at-risk areas.
Efforts have been made to reduce the emotional toll of isolation on children in Ebola treatment centers, including the creation of visibility areas where parents can see and communicate with their hospitalized children. But admission to an Ebola treatment center remains a deeply distressing experience for children, many of whom are too young to understand what is happening and why.
MSF has recruited and trained caregivers to provide daily support and comfort to children inside several MSF-supported Ebola treatment centers while wearing full PPE. These caregivers have a range of experience, including caring for Ebola survivors. Today, 13 caregivers are supporting children at Kitatumba Ebola treatment center in Butembo. While not a perfect solution, this initiative provides essential human contact and emotional support for children suffering from the disease.
Historically, children have often been excluded from clinical research or included only after significant delays, creating dangerous gaps in the evidence available to guide and improve their care and delaying access to potentially lifesaving interventions.
"On top of enormous challenges caring for young patients, medical [teams] are dealing with a lack of pediatric dosing guidance and limited availability of child-friendly formulations of investigational medicines," said Dr. Guyguy Manangama, epidemiologist and deputy director of operations at MSF. "A child-centered approach must be at the heart of medical care, operational planning, and research efforts."
In the ongoing Ebola outbreak in DR Congo, children with the disease are at a disproportionately higher risk of dying.
"Treatments, vaccines, and other preventive tools should be evaluated for use in children from the outset of research efforts and made available to them without delay," added Dr. Manangama. "Yet in the current outbreak, children are still being left behind, with very limited access to vaccination trials and campaigns, as well as the latest therapeutic innovations — despite bearing a significant burden of disease. Children cannot continue to wait for data generated from adults before benefiting from advances in Ebola care and prevention."
MSF urges national authorities, research institutions, pharmaceutical developers, and international funders to prioritize the inclusion of children in all ongoing and future Bundibugyo virus studies. Ensuring equitable access to research and new medical tools, including vaccines, is essential to reducing preventable deaths and improving outcomes for one of the most vulnerable groups.
The impact of the outbreak on children extends beyond Ebola infection itself. Disruptions to essential health services can rapidly increase the risks of vaccine-preventable diseases, malnutrition , and other common childhood illnesses. Preserving routine immunization, nutrition programs, and access to primary health care — while reducing the risk of Ebola transmission in health facilities — must be considered a core component of the outbreak response, not an afterthought.

articles.title_orig: Remains of Minnesota World War II veteran return home after more than 80 years
articles.title_zh: Remains of Minnesota World War II veteran return home after more than 80 years
articles.content_orig:
WEBSTER, Wis. (Northern News Now) - The remains of Ernest LaVerne Lund, a Minnesota World War II veteran who died in 1944 during the West Loch Disaster at Pearl Harbor, have returned home.
Lund was 28 years old and working aboard a Navy landing ship when he died. Federal officials identified him through DNA testing that matched his remains with family members.
His body arrived in Minneapolis from Honolulu on Thursday before being transported to Webster, Wisconsin, where a visitation will be held.
Lund will be buried Saturday in Markville, Minnesota, where his parents are buried.

articles.title_orig: Olympian gymnast Frederick Richard talks growing up in Stoughton and upcoming World Championships
articles.title_zh: Olympian gymnast Frederick Richard talks growing up in Stoughton and upcoming World Championships
articles.content_orig:
Frederick Richard , the 22-year-old gymnast from Stoughton, has earned many accolades in his early gymnastics career. He won a bronze medal during the Paris 2024 Summer Olympics and most recently became the second Black gymnast to win a men's all-around title .
As he vies for a spot on the U.S. men's gymnastics team in next year's Summer Olympics set for Los Angeles, he is first heading to Rotterdam in the Netherlands for the 2026 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships.
Richard spoke with WBUR's All Things Considered host Lisa Mullins before heading to Europe. He talked about what the upcoming championship means for him, learning gymnastics in Stoughton and what changes he hopes to see in the sport.
Below are highlights from their conversation, which have been lightly edited.
On the upcoming 2026 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships...
"It's the competition that decides whether all the work I've put in my whole life has finally gotten me to the highest level. When I say highest level, becoming number one in the world. This competition, World Championships, what they say is actually harder to win than the Olympics.
"You face the best in the world from any country, no matter how good or bad their country is. Whereas at the Olympics, they only let 18 countries in, and if your country isn't one of those 18, no matter how good you are, you can't compete in the Olympics."
On growing up in Stoughton and learning to love gymnastics...
"I started very, very young, probably 2 years old. ... My sister was doing it, but my parents just wanted a place nearby to drop me off to get rid of me for three hours, and I loved it there.
"I got lucky enough to have a coach there in that gym who believed in me, who didn't ask about payment, just took me to every gym across the state, drove me two hours on Saturdays to better facilities to get me to the highest level.
"I've just loved gymnastics my whole life. I just feel like it's just been this thing that's natural as walking to me. I learned to walk, and by the time I did that, I was already learning that gymnastics existed."
On his untraditional gymnastics uniform...
"So the old uniform is what you call a leotard, or girls call their piece a leotard. Guys have the same thing, which means you step into the one piece and it rides up your crotch. I think it's outdated. I think it's uncomfortable.
"I think it's time we wear stuff that are looser, especially when we train every day of the year in more comfortable, looser clothing.
"[My uniform is] more of a jersey instead of a one piece. Then it's shorts and leggings over the stirrups that hook over the feet. All that is to basically get me closer to what I'm comfortable training with every day."
Why he thinks it's worth wearing it instead of traditional gymnastics clothing...
"By the time you hit 10 or 12, you start to realize everybody else is doing basketball, football, soccer ... and you tell them you do gymnastics and they think, 'Oh, splits and cartwheels and leotards.' And I'm just like, 'That's not really what my sport is.' It's like this thing I fell in love with my whole life. And when you're a kid and you do want to be cool, you do want to fit in.
"I just remember the uniform as one of those pain points. 'Ah, I have to wear this every time I compete. Ah, this doesn't represent me. It doesn't represent really the thing that I love, but I'll just wear it because you have to.' And now that I'm older, now that I'm one of the people who get to lead where our sport goes, I think it's one of the things that need to change.
"I think all these small things do add up to our sport eventually being more liked by younger boys."
On his social media presence...
"I think gymnastics is a sport that very, very few people understand. Even now, when everybody watches the Olympics, no one really understands it of how are we scored, how do the rules work, how do the skills work.
"I feel like I got into social media for one big reason, and it is when no one really understands the sport you do, how can I actually make it still entertaining or make people still want to watch or make people actually understand the rules a little bit better? That's how it all started.
"I get to show it off, entertain people in different ways, and try to make them just understand gymnastics better, understand the things I'm going through in this journey, whether it's uniform or getting deducted or saluting or winning or, going to world championships and hopefully everything I've worked for pays off. I feel like that's what social media is and that's what this brand is."
This segment aired on October 15, 2026.
Lisa Mullins is the voice of WBUR’s All Things Considered. She anchors the program, conducts interviews and reports from the field.
Kevin Vu is WBUR's newsroom fellow.

articles.title_orig: Investors temper Anthropic IPO valuation expectations over revenue growth slowdown, sources say
articles.title_zh: Investors temper Anthropic IPO valuation expectations over revenue growth slowdown, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic's latest revenue figures were like chum in the water for the AI doomers.
Critics pointed to the revenue figure to argue the AI boom is ending.
Anthropic is getting ready to go public in what's expected to be a historic IPO.
Nearly $17 billion in quarterly revenue is good, right? Not if you're the most hotly anticipated IPO candidate in recent market history, apparently.
Anthropic, which is gearing up for what's expected to be a historic public offering, told investors this week that it made $16.8 billion last quarter . That's a significant jump from the prior three-month period, but slower than the growth rate from the first quarter to the second— and AI doomsayers dooming harder than ever.
Market researcher publication Geiger Capital shared a graphic of Anthopic's revenue run-rate on X, stating, "Not good enough. It's over."
Other prominent AI skeptics shared similar views. Gary Marcus, an AI researcher and author who has been an outspoken critic of the market's frenzy for AI, recalled a previous Anthropic revenue forecast, implying that it seems absurd now.
Marcus engaged with a user defending Anthropic, who argued that its slower Q3 growth was due to the "death of tokenmaxxing" and rising competition from Chinese open source models.
Tech founder and former US presidential candidate Andrew Yang, a fellow AI critic, highlighted the market implications of Anthropic's newly released figures, laying out what they might mean for other tech companies.
"Anthropic's quarterly revenue growth rate of ~45% is going to be seen as disappointing, and will put massive pressure on the AI hypergrowth story. If valuations start correcting, watch out below."
Citrini Research, the firm that went viral in February for publishing a hypothetical doomsday scenario that triggered a stock brief stock sell-off posted, "Oh it's over over" as Anthropic's revenue figures made the rounds.
Ed Zitron, an independent journalist and researcher who compared OpenAI to Lehman Brothers after auditing its financials, quickly chimed in after the figures were released.
"The absolute best thing about this story is that boosters are furious Anthropic didn't give a new magical made up run rate number," he wrote.
Zitron has been a steadfast AI doomsayer , repeatedly predicting that the bubble will burst, with consequences that extend far beyond the stock market.

articles.title_orig: Katie Zacharia Defends Calling Herself a Lawyer in New Interview
articles.title_zh: Katie Zacharia Defends Calling Herself a Lawyer in New Interview
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump's new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is defending her self-description as a lawyer, while acknowledging that she took the bar exam and considered the results "inconsequential."
Zacharia's legal qualifications have faced growing scrutiny since her debut White House media briefing earlier this week, when shortly afterward she was asked which state she passed the bar exam in and replied: " When I moved to China ."
In an interview Thursday with right-wing provocateur Jack Posobiec on Real America's Voice, she did not deny reports that she'd failed to pass the bar.
Zacharia, who moved to China after earning her law degree in 2011, told Posobiec she had already preregistered for the bar exam before moving to Beijing, where her husband was working at an American private equity firm.
"I didn't want to withdraw from that," Zacharia said of the bar exam. "And we knew we would be moving out to China, and I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I had been long-distance from for at least a year."
Zacharia said she thought she'd take the bar and "see what happens."
"The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn't need the bar in China, and we left shortly thereafter," said Zacharia.
The Wall Street Journal reported late Wednesday that Zacharia failed California's bar exam after graduating from Pepperdine University in 2011.
A Business Insider review of records for all 50 states and the District of Columbia found no evidence that Zacharia had been admitted to practice law in the US.
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
In China, Zacharia said she took a job in the international practice division of the Zhong Lun law firm, where she said she worked on multimillion-dollar shareholder agreements and cross-border transactions. She said she was one of four associates under a senior partner.
"After moving to China, I didn't really think much of the bar results or consider that something that I needed to focus on," Zacharia told Posobiec, adding, "There's no Chinese bar. I had enough credentials, which was my law degree, to be able to do this practice."
"I had all the necessary requirements to do that, and I was able to do it effectively and well," she said.
She also said that she never retook the bar exam after returning to the US and having the first of four children with her husband within six years.
Zacharia said she consulted with people within the legal field "for a very long time" and was told it would be acceptable to call herself a lawyer "and provide legal analysis, not legal advice."
"They said absolutely, absolutely across the board — you can call yourself a lawyer, you have a JD, and to buffer that, you have international legal experience in transactional law," Zacharia said.
"It's unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy," she said. "The truth is, I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney at law."
Zacharia's LinkedIn page says she served as general counsel for Fix California, a political advocacy group, between January 2024 and March 2025. In California, it is a misdemeanor to practice law or to advertise yourself as an attorney without a license.
At least two watchdog groups have filed a complaint about Zacharia with the State Bar of California this week.

articles.title_orig: Rick Kaplan Will Depart NAB
articles.title_zh: Rick Kaplan Will Depart NAB
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › People News
Rick Kaplan, a key figure at the National Association of Broadcasters for the past 14 years, will leave NAB at the end of the year.
For the last five years he has been NAB’s chief legal officer and EVP for legal and regulatory affairs, putting him at the elbow of President/CEO Curtis LeGeyt through some of NAB’s biggest issues.
The association also announced that in January it will bring its government relations and legal teams together under Shawn Donilon, who will be chief advocacy officer. LeGeyt called Donilon “a trusted leader and a skilled strategist.”
NAB said this structure will strengthen coordination between its advocacy on Capitol Hill, its interactions with the administration and its work with the Federal Communications Commission.
NAB had high praise for Rick Kaplan. President/CEO Curtis LeGeyt cited his ability to build consensus and his “tireless” advocacy.
According to the announcement text, Kaplan “led NAB through a decade of critical court wins, including a unanimous victory at the Supreme Court removing outdated restrictions on broadcast ownership. He also oversaw a seminal victory for the radio industry before the Copyright Royalty Board, which dramatically lowered streaming rates for broadcasters. That win paved the way for a landmark settlement in the most recent webcasting proceeding.”
NAB said he also worked on regulatory and legal issues including ATSC 3.0, retransmission consent, the FCC’s broadcast spectrum incentive auction, music licensing, sponsor ID rules and reducing broadcasters’ regulatory fees.
Prior to NAB, Kaplan held several roles at the FCC, including chief of the Wireless Telecommunications Bureau and counsel roles with Chairman Julius Genachowski and Commissioner Mignon Clyburn.

articles.title_orig: Partnership with World Wide Technology Raceway Opens Doors to Motor Sports Industry for First-Year Students
articles.title_zh: Partnership with World Wide Technology Raceway Opens Doors to Motor Sports Industry for First-Year Students
articles.content_orig:
The last few weeks have been exciting for students in the Rawlings Sport Business Management Program at Maryville University. Nearly 100 first-year students assisted in set-up and operations for both the NASCAR O’Reilly Auto Parts Series and Enjoy Illinois 300 NASCAR Cup Series Chase races held at the World Wide Technology Raceway in Madison, Il.
By design, Rawlings Sport Business Management students don’t just study the business of sport — they live it, and as raceway crew, they logged about 600 hours on-site during two set-up days, plus another 300 hours during event days. For many, this was their first opportunity to work in the industry.
Their impact on the success of the motor sport events did not go unnoticed.
“Rawlings Sport Business Management students are excellent, and we appreciate having them assist us with these national events,” said Declan O’Neil, vice president of partnership marketing at World Wide Technology Raceway.
Through such important experiential learning opportunities, students develop a wide range of industry skills. They also see how knowledge gained in the classroom plays out in the real world, said Daniel Schmidt, 10′, MBA ’16, instructor in the program.
“Their work at World Wide Technology Raceway involves corporate sponsorship, activation, event management and operations as well as ticketing and customer communication,” he said. “They also get exposed to motor sports — a part of the sports industry they’ve probably never considered before.”
Students appreciate the opportunity to practice skills, expand their resumes, build professional networks and discover first-hand what it takes to host a successful major event.
First-year student Karli Dean learned that being adaptable and paying attention to details is important. Student, Parker Medina, agreed. “The little details really go a long way when setting up these events,” Medina said. “Putting so much time and effort on the small things really shows how much the hosts care about their events as well as how much it means to the consumers and sponsors.”
Charlie Phillips, discovered the ticketing department involves much more than just selling tickets. “Ticketing covers a lot more to make sure fans are happy and have a great experience — so they’ll come back again and again,” said Phillips, a Rawlings Sport Business Management student.
Andra Alexander helped lead her team of fellow students as they hung scrim along fences on the racetrack as well as near fan engagement areas. “This really made me realize how much work gets put into any kind of event and is going to make me appreciate my experiences even more, whether I’m behind the scenes or in the stands,” Alexander said.
Erick Gates, who will enter the job market when he graduates in spring, understands the value of such opportunities. “Diversifying my resume with experiential experiences has been key,” he said.
The partnership with World Wide Technology Raceway has continued to deepen over the past seven years, says Schmidt, including both onsite and project-based learning opportunities as well as in-classroom sessions with executives of the raceway.
“Because of this partnership, we’ve had numerous students serve as interns and others hired as employees,” he said. “Our World Wide Technology Raceway opportunities are unique learning experiences specifically tied to the Rawlings Sport Business Management program, and we’re grateful for the confidence and trust they have in our students.”

Maryville offers over 90 degrees at the undergraduate, master’s and doctoral levels, as well as several certificates that align with the undergraduate and graduate education levels. Maryville is recognized as the third fastest-growing private university in the United States by The Chronicle of Higher Education, serving students from 50 states and 56 countries. articles.title_orig: CDC sending a ‘disease detective’ to help stop measles outbreak in Pennsylvania
articles.title_zh: CDC sending a ‘disease detective’ to help stop measles outbreak in Pennsylvania
articles.content_orig:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is sending one of its scientists to Pennsylvania to help curb the state’s growing measles outbreak , a CDC spokesperson said Thursday. That person, a “disease detective” within the agency’s Epidemic Intelligence Service, is scheduled to arrive later this week.
It’s the CDC’s first in-person assistance to the state after a social media feud in August between Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. The two traded jabs following a press briefing where Shapiro announced that two unvaccinated people had died of measles complications and accused Kennedy of spreading vaccine misinformation.
“I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania,” Shapiro said during the briefing.
Kennedy then suggested that the deaths may have been “fabricated,” and that Shapiro was seeking to profit from them politically.
Since August, six people diagnosed with measles have died in Pennsylvania, according to health officials and county coroners. The CDC has acknowledged two of the deaths on its measles outbreak website, saying the other measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania are “under review.”
“CDC will continue working closely with Pennsylvania health officials to provide the expertise and support needed to respond to the outbreak and protect public health,” a CDC spokesperson wrote in an email Thursday, adding that director Dr. Erica Schwartz recommends the MMR vaccine “as the most effective way to prevent measles and protect against infection.”
Pennsylvania is experiencing the nation’s worst measles outbreak in 30 years, with at least 1,222 confirmed cases and 225 hospitalizations, although doctors say the actual number of illnesses is likely much higher. The outbreak’s center remains in Lancaster County, but it is spreading across the state.
The Pennsylvania Department of Health did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the CDC aid.
The CDC team has previously sent teams to other states with large clusters of measles illnesses: Kansas, New Mexico, South Carolina, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin. Such deployments are usually short -term, about one to three weeks. They’re meant to help mobilize and streamline outbreak containment efforts.
In addition to the deployment, the CDC is releasing nearly $4 million to aid the measles response efforts in Pennsylvania.
Erika Edwards is a health and medical news writer and reporter for NBC News and "TODAY."

articles.title_orig: DOJ sues California, demands it purge voter rolls for alleged noncitizens
articles.title_zh: DOJ sues California, demands it purge voter rolls for alleged noncitizens
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Justice Department sued California on Thursday, alleging that the federal government has identified more than 20,000 noncitizens who are unlawfully registered to vote.
The lawsuit , filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, came after Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter sent letters to counties earlier this week, including Los Angeles, ordering them to review a list of names of suspected noncitizens who he alleged received mail-in ballots for the upcoming midterm elections.
"State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement announcing the lawsuit.
"If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government."
In the letter that McCotter sent to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk, he enclosed a password-protected thumb drive that he said contained names compiled by the Department of Homeland Security, and imposed a 48-hour deadline for the clerk's office to review the list.
Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder and clerk, said in a statement responding to McCotter's demands that the county would not be reviewing the materials on the thumb drive because doing so would conflict with "established data privacy and information security protocols." He said the device was not considered a "secure medium."
Secretary of State Shirley Weber, meanwhile, said the Justice Department had not provided the list of names and blasted the Trump administration for what it said were "unsubstantiated claims" that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls.
In Thursday's lawsuit, the Justice Department accused the state of failing to work with the federal government to correct the alleged problems with its voter rolls.
"The Federal Government asked California to work collaboratively to identify any noncitizens registered to vote in the State. California made no serious effort to do so," the lawsuit said.
"The United States thus seeks commonplace election relief when a ballot is called into question. This Court should enjoin California from presently tabulating vote-by-mail ballots from likely noncitizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined," it added.
In a statement provided to CBS News, the California Secretary of State's office said, "Due to the pending litigation, we have no further information we can share regarding the matter." It directed CBS News to its news release on the situation and Weber's letter to McCotter.
CBS News has also reached out to the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk for comment.
The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division has filed 31 lawsuits in an effort to force states to hand over unredacted copies of their voter rolls. The division has said it wants to ensure states are keeping clean voter lists, but it has since acknowledged that it also intends to share the data with the Department of Homeland Security so that the lists can be screened for noncitizens.
Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general for the Civil Rights Division, sent letters to all 50 states in July threatening to take criminal action if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls.
So far, the Justice Department has lost 26 of those cases, and has not achieved one legal victory to date.
It has resorted to using publicly available voter lists and other investigative means to try to identify noncitizens who may be registered in those states.

Steven Burrell, a fourth year on the Virginia wrestling team, is set to compete at the U23 World Championships this weekend in Las Vegas, Nevada. Burrell will represent Jamaica and compete in men’s freestyle at 92kg.
CHARLOTTESVILLE, Va. – Steven Burrell, a fourth year on the Virginia wrestling team, is set to compete at the U23 World Championships this weekend in Las Vegas, Nevada. Burrell will represent Jamaica and compete in men’s freestyle at 92kg. The weekend competition at the Thomas & Mack Center begins on Friday (Oct. 16) with qualification rounds beginning at 10:30 a.m. Should he advance, the semifinal rounds are at 4:45 p.m., while the medal rounds will be at 6 p.m. on Saturday (Oct. 17). All times are local to Las Vegas. Fans can keep up with the action or stream it through FloWrestling.com. Burrell has previously found success on the national and international stage, taking third at the U20 U.S. Championships in 2024. In high school, he was a US Open All-American and NHSCA All-American. Last season for the Cavaliers, he defeated a pair of nationally-ranked opponents in No. 14 Jack Wehmeyer of Columbia and No. 25 Patrick Brophy in dual action against NC State.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia, Apple each gave $25 million for Trump's ballroom, Washington Post reports
articles.title_zh: Nvidia, Apple each gave $25 million for Trump's ballroom, Washington Post reports
articles.content_orig:
A list obtained by The Washington Post reveals all the major donors to President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project, including previously undisclosed contributors who have benefited from regulatory decisions, government contracts and, in one case, a pardon for a family member.
Tech giants Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million, the top contribution amount, the list shows. The Adelson family, one of the GOP’s largest donor dynasties, committed that sum as well, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network.
Absent from the list is Trump himself, who has said that he is helping to pay for the project. “It’s being paid for a hundred percent by me and some friends of mine,” he said last year, days after demolition began on the old East Wing.
The White House publicly identified 37 people, companies and foundations as donors last October, without revealing the amount of their individual gifts.
The list obtained by The Post, an internal spreadsheet used to track contributions for the fundraising effort, contains the source, date and amount of all 67 donations above $10,000 recorded as of late last month. It shows a total of $333 million from private donors, aligning with the administration’s public statements. Additional records, also internal to the fundraising effort, provide more detail about the donations and indicate that at least $77 million came from donors who requested anonymity.
The list and other documents offer a panoramic view of a fundraising campaign that is extraordinary both for its size and opacity. Ordinary political giving requires public disclosure and is subject to campaign finance rules. The ballroom donations are collected by a nonprofit and then channeled to the government and into a White House account the president directly controls.
Independent experts and scholars have expressed alarm at the potential the arrangement has for influence buying and coerced giving.
Some donors on the list obtained by The Post cut large checks, while others created installment plans that are still being paid off, the additional records show. The list does not include in-kind contributions.
The Post’s reporting does not establish a connection between the donation commitments and favorable actions by the Trump administration. But the documents show that the vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government.
Companies or executives of firms that have had contracts with the federal government during Trump’s second term accounted for about half of the total, The Post found.
After reviewing the list obtained by The Post, White House spokesman Davis Ingle declined to discuss individual donations but described the ballroom donors as “a wide array of great American companies and generous individuals, all of whom are contributing to make the People’s House better for generations to come.”
“The same critics who are alleging fake conflicts of interests, would also complain if American taxpayers were footing the bill for these long-overdue renovations,” he said. He added that the administration will “relentlessly pursue those responsible for this cowardly leak while continuing to protect all those who give.”
The Post is publishing the names of the 57 donors listed as having committed to giving $100,000 or more. The additional records detailing donors’ preferences show at least nine wanted to remain anonymous.
The Post attempted to reach all the donors whose names appear in this report. Most did not respond or declined to comment. Those who did comment said that there was no connection between their donations and any favorable government actions.
Nvidia, the world’s most valuable public company, became a top contributor to the ballroom in October 2025, nearly three months after it struck a groundbreaking pact with Trump to sell advanced microchips to China despite national security concerns.
CEO Jensen Huang told reporters at the time that the company was contributing to Trump’s ballroom “in a small way” but did not provide a dollar amount. Documents show Nvidia requested that its $25 million donation be kept anonymous.
“As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said in response to questions from The Post. “We were proud to be able to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans and have said so publicly since the donation was made.”
Major GOP donor Joseph Popolo Jr., Trump’s ambassador to the Netherlands, and his wife contributed $1 million from their family fund to support the ballroom project in late 2025, the records show. Their donation - made two months after Popolo’s confirmation - has not been previously reported.
Trump Cabinet member Kelly Loeffler of the Small Business Administration and her husband Jeff Sprecher, former chairman of the New York Stock Exchange, promised $5 million for the project, the list shows. Brandon Lutnick, chairman of investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald and the son of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, donated stock worth more than $2.5 million, the records show.
Popolo, Loeffler, Sprecher and the Lutnicks did not respond to requests for comment.
More than three-quarters of the money for the ballroom came in commitments of $5 million or more. Among the top donors are some of America’s blue-chip companies, including Amazon, Caterpillar, Comcast, Microsoft and T-Mobile. (Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos owns The Post . )
Cryptocurrency companies, now under loosened regulations from the Trump administration, and their investors promised more than $18 million. The largest portion came from Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss, co-founders of the Gemini crypto exchange, who together donated bitcoin valued at $5,050,018, the records show.
The Winklevoss brothers did not respond to requests for comment.
The ballroom project has also received dozens of small contributions, some as low as $10. The list and additional documents show the source of all but $24,000 of the total donations.
The total fundraising amount falls short of the $400 million Trump has said he intends to raise for the work. The cost of building the new East Wing, which includes the ballroom, office space and an underground military facility, was projected in March to have increased to $600 million, an estimate previously reported by The Post. The White House has used taxpayer dollars to cover some of the construction cost, records show.
The ballroom donations are routed through the Trust for the National Mall, a D.C.-based nonprofit whose mission is to restore and preserve the National Mall and the White House grounds. Nonprofits are not generally required to disclose their donors.
Prospective donors were sent a “pledge agreement form,” a copy of which was obtained by The Post, for giving toward the “Donald J. Trump Ballroom.” The form lists Meredith O’Rourke, the top fundraiser for Trump’s 2024 campaign, as the main contact.
O’Rourke referred questions to the White House.
A 12-page agreement between the government and the Trust requires that the Trust “maintain the anonymity of Project donors to the extent provided by law and not publicly recognize any such donor unless explicitly authorized in writing” by staff in the White House’s Executive Residence unit.
Democratic lawmakers have denounced the fundraising for the ballroom as secretive and potentially transactional. They have demanded that the administration and the Trust provide details about the donors and circumstances of the gifts. Those demands have been rebuffed.
In a statement the Trust said: “In philanthropy, it is not uncommon for donors to request their gifts remain anonymous. The Trust is committed to honoring donors requesting anonymity.”

articles.title_orig: Our model puts us within 'shooting distance' of China's AI models, says Reflection CEO
articles.title_zh: Our model puts us within 'shooting distance' of China's AI models, says Reflection CEO
articles.content_orig:
Tim Cook and Mark Zuckerberg have clashed for years, but with John Ternus taking the reins at Apple , the rivals are finding common ground in artificial intelligence.
Meta and Apple revealed a new collaboration Thursday that will enable developers to easily run Meta's new open-weight AI model on Apple's high-end desktop computers.
The collaboration centers on Muse Spark Open, the most capable open-weight model released under a license that allows for limited commercial use, according to Meta. It's an 816-billion-parameter model using a so-called mixture-of-experts architecture . As an open-weight model, developers can download the technology's parameters, or weights, from the internet and run the model on a wide range of hardware.
Customers will be able to pair between two and four Mac Studio PCs to use Muse Spark to code, analyze video or do other agentic work. The model runs locally, instead of in the cloud, adding a layer of security and saving users money, the companies said.
Thursday's announcement, following months of collaboration, is a sign that the AI boom has shifted historical alliances in Silicon Valley. For years, Apple and Meta regarded each other warily and avoided public partnerships, and the relationship hit rock bottom after Apple introduced privacy changes in 2021 that limited the targeting capabilities of digital ad companies. Meta estimated in early 2022 that the change would cut its revenue that year by $10 billion.
Representatives from Apple and Meta declined to say if the Muse Spark Open collaboration was the start of a deeper relationship.
Zuckerberg posted a picture on X showing the Meta agent working on a Mac computer. He wrote, "Muse Spark Open -- weights releasing today -- runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with @johnternus and Apple."
Ternus responded , "Congrats to the team! Amazing to run a model of Muse Spark Open's caliber and scale this efficiently, right from your desk. Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI!"
Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview that many powerful open-weight models are too big to be run on the majority of personal computers, but Apple's Mac Studios make enough memory available to users so that it's practical to run Muse Spark Open.
The move represents an important show of confidence in Meta's rebooted AI efforts and could pose a challenge to OpenAI and Anthropic. It could also signal Apple's growing strength in AI chips, a market that Nvidia has dominated so far due to their prevalence in large data centers.
" We worked with Apple to bring leading Agent capabilities to your desktop for the first time on the Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios, so you know we're really excited about this," Wang said. Developers can download a version of the AI model from websites like Hugging Face without extra configuration for Apple's silicon. Muse Spark Open has also been tuned to run faster on Apple's hardware, and the iPhone maker revealed new benchmarks for its chips and published technical documentation about its MLX AI framework's ability to split open-source models across multiple machines.
Mac Studios aren't cheap though, and this AI model requires the fastest Apple chips and as much memory as possible.
Currently, a Mac Studio with the required M5 Ultra chip and 256GB of memory costs at least $10,799. A more expensive version with 512GB of RAM will be released later this month.
Plus, users will need to buy multiple machines.
The two companies are collaborating on open-source AI, which has become a point of contention in Washington as politicians worry that free Chinese models could undercut American AI. Although Meta once centered its AI strategy on its older open-weight Llama family of models , it has since focused on creating proprietary models under the leadership of Wang , who joined Meta when the company invested more than $14 billion into his former startup Scale AI last year.
While Apple and Meta, then known as Facebook, partnered on iPhone extensions over a decade ago, they haven't struck any public partnerships since 2017 after Apple removed system-level Facebook integration from the iPhone.
"Most of the animosity predates my tenure at the company, but obviously there's been a long history between Meta and Apple," Wang said, pointing to one member of his team, AI researcher and former Apple director Daniel Gross, as a reason for the collaboration. Gross, along with former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman , was a major Zuckerberg hire last year as the Facebook founder was overhauling his company's AI strategy.
Their leaders have also traded harsh words.
Cook, who was Apple CEO until Ternus succeeded him last month, took a shot at Zuckerberg in 2018, during the Cambridge Analytica scandal, saying, "I wouldn't be in this situation." Cook often criticized Meta for compromising user privacy.
Zuckerberg has also insulted Apple in public, telling Joe Rogan last year that the company "hasn't invented anything great since the iPhone." Zuckerberg has long sought to find a platform that Meta can own so it's not beholden to Apple.
Ternus, a hardware engineer, has already started changing things at Apple, including when it releases products.
And Meta's developers haven't been able to resist Apple's products. The company bought hundreds of Mac computers so its Superintelligence team could experiment with local AI and agents earlier this year.
Meta is just the latest AI model developer to team up with Apple.
In 2024, Apple announced a partnership with OpenAI to integrate ChatGPT into Siri, although the integration " dramatically underperformed " and didn't lead to OpenAI user growth, OpenAI said in a filing that's part of a legal dispute with Elon Musk 's xAI. Apple sued OpenAI in July, alleging trade secret theft, a claim OpenAI denied.
Earlier this year, Apple announced a deal with Google , to use its Gemini models in Apple Intelligence as well as Google Cloud infrastructure.
Still, Apple's AI strategy has drawn criticism from investors and customers in part because its new version of Siri, released last month, isn't as advanced as chatbots and agents from leading labs.
Meanwhile, Meta has bet big on becoming a leading lab but has struggled to keep up with the competition and its business remains almost entirely reliant on ads. Recent developments, such as Meta's Muse personal agent app and its latest proprietary foundation model, Muse Wonder, released earlier this week, have begun to excite investors who are optimistic about new AI business opportunities.
Open source remains part of Zuckerberg's AI strategy. In August, Meta debuted a small open-weight AI model dubbed Muse Glimmer , with Zuckerberg pledging to eventually release something bigger and more powerful.
Muse Spark Open isn't as advanced as Muse Wonder, a proprietary offering, but Wang said it's good enough to potentially entice more coders to upgrade.
"These aren't the most capable models that we've developed or released," Wang said. "But we think that there will be a lot of companies and developers who sort of use this model and tinker with it at small scale and then seek to ramp up and scale up their usage."

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: S&P 500 rises as tech stocks pare losses; Nasdaq turns higher, Dow advances as Treasury yields drop
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: S&P 500 rises as tech stocks pare losses; Nasdaq turns higher, Dow advances as Treasury yields drop
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose on Thursday as concerns around tech companies overspending on artificial intelligence led investors to rotate out of the trade and seek value elsewhere. Traders also digested U.S. data that pointed to persistent inflation.
The blue-chip index added 556.21 points, or 1.08%, to end at 52,177.69. The S&P 500 gained 0.33% to close at 7,744.06. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite closed up 0.08% at 26,713.03, rebounding from session lows. At one point, the index was down 1.4% on the day.
Seagate Technology and Western Digital added to their declines this week, along with shares of SK Hynix , which drove a rout in South Korea's Kospi index overnight. Traders were becoming concerned about a potential memory chip glut as South Korea faces increasing competition from China. Tesla CEO Elon Musk discussed the matter in a post on X , saying that "China will be making a LOT of RAM in 2028."
Compounding worries in the AI space, sources told CNBC that Anthropic's revenue grew to $16.8 billion in the third quarter, with some traders concerned the AI giant's top line might not be growing fast enough to justify the lofty gains in chipmakers.
However, other stocks in the AI trade recovered. CoreWeave shares gained almost 6%, reversing course from the prior day's losses. The stock tumbled more than 15% in the previous session as investors grew fearful that the company was borrowing too much for its AI build-out. CoreWeave corporate bond yields also surged . Additionally, Micron Technology rebounded from earlier losses to gain nearly 2%.
"When Treasurys are yielding 5% and that's the highest since the early 2000s, investors are going to start weighing that versus taking a huge bet on on AI," said Alex Shahidi, co-CIO of MAI Capital Management's Evoke. "It's not are you in or out of AI; it's how concentrated you want to be."
The market was supported by gains in areas outside of tech. Shares of retailer Walmart climbed 1.5%, while Nike shares jumped more than 5%.
Investors also reacted to more insights on the inflation front. The September reading on producer prices recorded an increase of 1.3% on the month and 6.3% year over year — the biggest monthly and yearly gains since 2022.
Concerns that the Federal Reserve could tighten monetary policy more aggressively before year-end weighed on equities Wednesday after new data showed consumer prices in September rose faster than expected on a year-over-year basis.
"Today's PPI report, after Wednesday's CPI, confirms inflation is getting worse as energy prices stay high," said David Russell, global head of market strategy at TradeStation. "Election or no election, prices are rising and the Fed might be forced to act."
The three major averages finished Thursday's session with gains.
The S&P 500 rose 0.33% to end at 7,744.06, while the Nasdaq Composite gained just 0.08% to 26,713.03. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 556.21 points, or 1.08%, to 52,177.69.
Analysts at Barclays say they're seeing signs that a SpaceX - Tesla merger is something that executives are thinking about, analysts with Barclays said Wednesday.
"We believe recent management comments indicate they see key benefits of a combination," analyst Dan Levy wrote to clients in a Wednesday note, though he didn't get into the details.
Vertical integration of production pipelines for two the companies, in addition to the elimination of overhead redundancies, would boost value added, Levy said. He put the Texas-based Terafab data center, which is already structured as a joint venture, at the center of his estimation.
"We see Terafab as a key driver of the potential combination as CEO Elon Musk strongly believes that Terafab will be required to support TSLA/SPCX compute needs," he wrote.
Performance is broadening out within the S&P 500.
More than half of S&P 500 stocks are trading above their 200-day moving averages, an improvement from  less than 40% at the end of September when gains were more concentrated, likely within tech stocks.
Some of the names moving above their 200-day moving averages for the first time in more than a month were Walmart ( WMT ), Kroger ( KR ), HCA Healthcare ( HCA ) and United Health Services ( UHS ).
— Nick Wells and Tobias Burns
CoreWeave stock broke into black in Thursday afternoon, trading up 3.5% just as of 2:53 p.m., after being down as much as 9.5% in morning trading.
The uptick proved a Wednesday Deutsche Bank note to be prescient. Analyst Brad Zelnick said that Wednesday's dislocation was "presenting buying opportunity."
"If this is purely about broader AI financing concerns, we'd argue CoreWeave continues to scale rather responsibly," he wrote to clients. "Near-term liquidity is in decent shape."
The stock got hit with a combination blow on Wednesday, with higher-than-expected inflation data initially pushing up bond yields, industrial titans fretting about the stock online, and some warnings from analysts about its sector.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) is lower for an eighth straight trading day, its first eight-day slide since September 2015; it fell for nine sessions in May 2006. The ETF has fallen more than 15% over that stretch. The fund was last down around 2%.
The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) is also down an eighth straight day, making it the longest slide since May 2006 when it fell for nine straight sessions.
— Sarah Min and Nick Wells
More than half of S&P 500 constituents are trading above their 200-day moving averages, a notable improvement from late September when that figure was around 40%.
The shift suggests that participation in the market's advance is broadening beyond recent high flyers of the AI trade. The 200-day moving average is a widely watched indicator of a stocks' long-term trend and a shift above that level can show improving momentum.
Among the names moving above their 200-day moving averages for the first time in a month are Walmart , Kroger , HCA Healthcare and Universal Health Services .
Wall Street firm Baird upgraded Bank of America to outperform from neutral Thursday, while maintaining its $62 price target, implying a 21% upside from its Wednesday close of $51.
The higher rerating on the bank comes despite it reporting a soft quarter before the open Thursday.
Bank of America delivered an earnings per share miss and weak noninterest income along with higher expenses on Wednesday, sending shares lower.
Baird called the sell-off "overdone" and sees the stock's weakness as a buying opportunity. That stems from the firm's view that the bank's 2027 net interest income outlook is an "incremental positive" coupled with the stock's attractive valuation.
Gil Luria, analyst at DA Davidson, said Anthropic's revenue for the third quarter was "not what anyone wanted to see."
Sources told CNBC that the AI giant's revenue grew to $16.8 billion in the third quarter , up from its second-quarter revenue of $11.6 billion. But, that growth in the third quarter was slower than its rise in the previous one, as first-quarter revenue for the company was just $4.7 billion.
Luria said, though, that there was good news as the Financial Times reported that Antrhopic had positive cash flow in the third quarter, pushing back on the narrative that the AI labs can't get to profitability. But he added that investors shouldn't be looking at a single company to judge the performance of the sector, and rather focus on corporate and consumer spending on the technology.
"We expect the overall market for AI spend to continue on a steep path as it diversifies away from Anthropic and OpenAI," he wrote in a Thursday note. "These two will see their market get cut from providing all-encompassing AI services to only providing frontier tokens for mission critical cost-insensitive applications… This overall demand should support more AI compute demand and more data center construction, even if it doesn't meet the most outlandish extrapolations."

articles.title_orig: Ilhan Omar's husband snaps over rumors she fled US after federal immigration fraud raid
articles.title_zh: Ilhan Omar's husband snaps over rumors she fled US after federal immigration fraud raid
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Ilhan Omar's, D-Minn., husband, Tim Mynett, responds to rumors that the congresswoman fled the country after HSI raided their Washington, D.C., home as part of a federal criminal investigation. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
While Ilhan Omar , D-Minn., has not been seen publicly since federal agents raided her Washington, D.C., residence on Monday, her political consultant husband was once again spotted emerging from their shared rental home this week.
Tim Mynett was seen Wednesday stepping out in the neighborhood to walk their Golden Labrador Retriever dog Teddy, a second time later that same day to take out the trash and a third time to walk out his wife's staffer.
"There are rumors that the congresswoman left the country, is that true?" Mynett was asked while on an evening walk with Teddy.
"You guys are annoying the hell out of all the neighbors around here, man," he told Fox News Digital when approached about the developments this week, including President Donald Trump weighing in on the saga.
One of Omar's congressional staffers was captured the same day bringing into the couple's home two large bags from fast food chain Burger King. Security escorted her to the door and staked out in front of the house after she entered with the meal.
ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION
An image of Ilhan Omar overlaid over her neighborhood in DC. (Getty Images)
Rumors swirled that Omar fled from the country following the raid carried out by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) as part of a criminal fraud investigation looking into the Somali-born congresswoman’s immigration paperwork, as first reported by Fox News Digital.
Omar’s cellphone and passport were reportedly seized by federal authorities during the search.
The congresswoman's staff helped to get her birth year adjusted from 1981 to 1982 in the Minnesota Legislative Reference Library, according to reporters. Omar gained citizenship automatically through her father’s naturalization since she was reportedly 17 years old at the time. If Omar was born in 1981, she would have been 18 years old, meaning the validity of her citizenship could be threatened because she was no longer a minor.
The altered birthdate was published during her entire time serving in Minnesota’s House and for months into her time serving in Congress.
When asked about the federal investigation earlier this week, Mynett told Fox News Digital he has "no concerns" about what federal authorities will find on his wife while investigating her immigration pathway.
"My wife came here when she was 12 years old as a child war refugee," Mynett said. "No concerns."
His comments to Fox News Digital come after Omar’s relatives were reportedly issued subpoenas as part of HSI’s investigation into the congresswoman's immigration paperwork. At least two of Omar's relatives were subpoenaed, one of which is reportedly Omar’s sister, Sahra Noor.
ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION
Fox News Digital asked Mynett about President Donald Trump publicly questioning Omar’s net worth by alleging on Truth Social that her accountant may have reported fraudulent money when her previous financial disclosure listed the couple's shared net worth as high as $30 million.
"Why did Ilhan Omar report a Net Worth of up to 30 Million Dollars just a short time ago, and then immediately say, "Oh, I made a mistake! It’s really $100,000." Could it be that her highly paid accountant actually reported the money that was stolen from her fraudulent activities in Minnesota? Would something like that be possible? Do you think the accountant actually gave the right number the first time, 30 Million Dollars, and then she was forced to disavow because she never would have been able to report where that much money came from? She must have freaked out when she saw that money!" Trump posted to Truth Social on Tuesday.
"Where did her house come from, where did her cars come from, and what about her lovely place in Washington, D.C.? I didn’t know that Congressmen and women made that kind of money, but I do know her husband, according to information and belief, makes almost nothing, so it couldn’t have come from him. How many people did she illegally bring into our Country from Somalia? America wants answers, and we want them, NOW!"
Mynett is at the center of yet another investigation into Omar — this time looking into her finances.
Following Monday’s HSI raid, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said Tuesday that her office is also investigating Omar's financial disclosures about reporting of her and Mynett’s shared net worth.

Rep. Ilhan Omar sits with husband Tim Mynett during the first day of the Democratic National Convention at the United Center on August 19, 2024, in Chicago, Illinois. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
Scrutiny of Omar's finances intensified after her 2024 congressional financial disclosure listed business interests associated with Mynett valued between $6 million and $30 million. Omar's office subsequently said the figures were incorrect and amended the filing.
The largest change in the documents was from Mynett’s assets . His reported ownership interests in both his winery and venture capital advisory firm, which were previously valued in the millions of dollars, are listed with no value now.
In Omar’s 2024 financial disclosure records, Mynett’s share in his winery was valued between $1 million and $5 million, and his share at the venture capital advisory firm was valued between $5 million and $25 million. Now, his equity interests are both listed at $0.
Omar's office previously told Fox News Digital that Mynett has partners in both businesses and said the earlier disclosure mistakenly reflected the businesses' total equity rather than his ownership interest. The office also said the original filing listed assets without accounting for liabilities.
