articles.title_orig: Capitol agenda: Some Republicans write off the House - Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Capitol agenda: Some Republicans write off the House - Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
The Republican Party’s midterm campaign has turned into a triage operation just three weeks out from November, as officials race to avert losses in a string of once-safe seats that they increasingly fear could cost them total control of Congress.
The worsening landscape has alarmed GOP operatives across several battleground states, forcing the party to pour resources into traditionally red districts and states at the expense of their once-expansive ambitions in Democratic areas.
And after months of pressing President Donald Trump to ramp up his travel on behalf of key candidates, some Republicans now worry he’s grown so unpopular that his presence on the campaign trail may in some cases be doing more harm than good.
One House Republican running for re-election said of the president’s numbers: “Trump is dragging the party down.”
The grim outlook gripping the GOP follows weeks of polling showing Republicans on track to lose the House amid intense voter anger over the Iran war and rising cost of living — and at grave risk of losing their once-solid majority in the Senate as well.
The widening number of competitive races has complicated Republican leaders’ plans to make up ground by unleashing hundreds of millions of dollars down the stretch. Despite a massive cash advantage fueled in part by pro-Trump super PAC, MAGA Inc., the spending so far has failed to significantly shift Republicans’ fortunes as more money gets diverted toward races once counted on as comfortable wins.
Already, the Senate Leadership Fund, the top GOP super PAC in Senate races, has suspended its ad reservations in North Carolina and plowed at least $10 million into Kansas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. It also recently invested $5 million in South Carolina to boost incumbent Sen. Darline Graham amid concerns among some Republicans she’s losing ground to Democrat Annie Andrews in the deep red state.
That’s on top of the more than $100 million that the Senate Leadership Fund has spent in Texas to boost Ken Paxton, who is scrambling to shore up GOP support in his race with Democrat James Talarico after a bruising primary campaign. Trump himself has now traveled to Texas three times in one month to rally voters on Paxton’s behalf.
“We were all hoping the war was going to be over now, but it’s not,” said one Trump adviser. “We shouldn’t have a fight in a place like Texas, but obviously we do.”
‘You don’t work, you don’t eat’: How voters feel about today’s high prices
Top Republicans steering spending on the House side are also expected to narrow their focus in the coming days, doubling down on races they see as winnable while slashing their investment in candidates whose fortunes are fading, multiple people familiar with the matter said.
That winnowing will mark the latest acknowledgment of the challenge facing Republicans — and an effort to concentrate resources on the select candidates capable of defending their seats, or flipping blue districts, and limiting Democrats’ encroachment overall.
The Cook Political Report dealt the latest blow on Friday, moving 18 House races toward Democrats. Those contests include five toss-up seats across Iowa, Pennsylvania and Washington that the closely watched analysis projects the Democratic candidates are now more likely to win.
The Senate map has also provided little reassurance for the GOP. Paxton is suffering a drip-drip of damaging audio leaks from a private fundraiser , further frustrating Republican officials who already believe he’s running a poor campaign. Democrats hold polling leads in swing states like Georgia and North Carolina, while making insurgent runs in solidly red states like Alaska and even Kansas.
“I don’t know that the environment could possibly get worse than it is,” said Jason Roe, a Michigan GOP strategist advising Rep. Tom Barrett, who is in a neck-and-neck race against Democratic challenger Will Lawrence. “If we lose this, it couldn’t have been won.”
Inside the White House, Trump and his top advisers are clear-eyed about the difficult odds of keeping the House and the rising threat to the Senate majority, people familiar with the matter said.
But there is still optimism that Republicans can limit their losses and turn the prospect of a blue wave into little more than a ripple. Trump advisers expect the polls to tighten in swing races in the campaign’s final days, especially as more ads hit the airwaves and less-engaged Republican voters begin to tune in.
“I’m not saying we are going to f***ing win, it is going to be so great. No, I am not saying that. But do we get wiped out? No, we aren’t gonna get wiped out,” said another House Republican running for re-election.
Some strong GOP candidates are likely to outperform the generic ballot polling that shows Democrats favored by a healthy margin, the people familiar argued. At the same time, they’re counting on a handful of far-left Democratic candidates to underperform. And even at the current margins, they note, the difference between Republicans losing the House or expanding their majority is only a matter of a few percentage points across a handful of races.
“This election is going to come down to one side saying Republicans have not cleaned their mess up fast enough, and what we are saying is, ‘We know you are struggling, but these are the things we are doing to make your life better and, by the way, they are crazy,” another Republican told CNN.
For his part, Speaker Mike Johnson has vowed to do everything he can to hold the majority and is campaigning in more than 40 districts and 20 states leading up to the election.
“Speaker Johnson is not slowing down and helping to get resources to every district that will decide the majority,” Johnson’s political communications director, Greg Steele, said in a statement to CNN.
While Trump has largely steered clear of swing districts of late, he has shown newfound enthusiasm for the campaign trail that his advisers have rushed to take advantage of, sending him to favorable areas across the country where they believe he can help GOP turnout. They’ve shrugged off any talk of Trump needing to lay low given his sagging approval ratings, arguing that the midterms are going to be a referendum on his presidency no matter what.
“The panic is unwarranted and it’s unfounded,” one White House official said of the GOP’s midterm trajectory. “It’s all going to come down to who has the ability to turn out their low-propensity voters. … That’s why we’re going where we’re going: To jazz up the base.”
In a statement, White House spokesman Davis Ingle called Trump “the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party.”
National Republican Congressional Committee spokesman Mike Marinella said in a statement, “House Republicans have a more favorable map, a stronger ground game, historic fundraising and spending advantages and battle-tested incumbents while Democrats are stuck dragging their unelectable socialist nominees across the finish line.”
A senior Republican National Committee official argued that pollsters and strategists are writing off the GOP’s chances in the midterms too soon.
“The first ones to rush and get on the phone with you all in these times are not the ones in the fight,” the official told CNN. “They would rather just say nobody knows what they are doing and everything is doomed than take an objective look at what is happening.”
Trump’s rallies — which included a stop in Texas on Thursday and a trip to upstate New York on Friday to stump for gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman — have bolstered Trump’s mood and view of Republicans’ chances, the White House official and others familiar with his comments said.
Nevertheless, Trump has tacitly acknowledged that his presence may not be helpful everywhere at a time when large majorities are frustrated with his economic policies and oppose the Iran war.
The president has declined to rebuke GOP candidates who have broken wit

articles.title_orig: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam
articles.title_zh: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam
articles.content_orig:
Nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own Game Store and launcher, the Fortnite maker is deploying a new tool to give it an edge over Valve: vibe coding.
In announcing the new publicly available “Preview” build of its Epic Games Launcher, Epic writes that “programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look.” And while that might sound a little tongue-in-cheek, Epic Games Store General Manager and VP Martin Keely told PC Gamer that the team “started from scratch” and used AI as “a tool to write and review new features and new capabilities from the ground up in a different tech stack than what we had previously.” The goal, Keely said, was to “look at functionality that existed [in the current Epic Games Launcher] and [say] we want to replicate that, but not the code itself.”
Speaking to IGN , Keely clarified that using AI to code the new Launcher “made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms, support Windows and Mac, and we’re going to have a Linux version as well.”
We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy.
Don’t believe us? Test it out for yourself in Preview: https://t.co/pdtAeEIri4 https://t.co/aMxojUUVPV
— Epic Games Store (@EpicGames) October 14, 2026
The focus on startup speed extends to Epic’s social media announcement , which once again stresses that “we vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy.” Ars’s own testing confirms that the new Launcher goes from a cold start to the store page a few seconds faster than Steam (assuming no login or update issues get in the way). Epic also claims the new Launcher can restore from the system tray to the Library screen slightly faster than Steam, though the claimed difference of 0.06 seconds in this seems so small as to be unnoticeable (and was in our testing).
Epic announced a ground-up “storefront rearchitecture” and “Launcher V2 private Beta” in an Unreal Fest presentation in June . At the time, the company said the new Launcher would have “5x faster cold start” times and help solve challenges that “every developer in this room and every player” has experienced with the current Launcher.
The term “vibe coding” still carries heavy connotations of quickly thrown-together slop that could hide crucial errors beneath the surface. On social media, Epic warns that its Launcher Preview “will have some bugs” that early testers can help squash with a feedback form. The announcement post also warns that the vibe-coded Preview is currently “light on features”— an FAQ clarifies that “certain social features and account management options” haven’t made it over from the legacy version just yet.
That said, the new Preview launcher adds some long-requested features like a Recent Games list and a centralized downloads hub for tracking network activity. And Epic writes that it is “working toward feature parity” between the new Launcher and the old one.
Epic’s release of the new “vibe coded” Launcher preview comes just days after a Bloomberg report suggesting the company is pivoting to an “AI first” development model for an upcoming Star Wars and Marvel-themed shooter. “We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media on Monday. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.”

articles.title_orig: GOP gets another Supreme Court win in TV political ad fight
articles.title_zh: GOP gets another Supreme Court win in TV political ad fight
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court again sided with Republicans on Wednesday in the latest clash over a new Federal Communications Commission policy that gives party committees access to discounted TV and radio advertising rates long available to political candidates.
The court agreed to ‌let the FCC, which is chaired by Trump ally Brendan Carr, avoid a judicially imposed deadline that would have forced the agency to rule ‌on a Democratic challenge to the policy before the November 3 midterm elections. The FCC joined two Republican committees in filing a request to the Supreme Court to lift the lower court's deadline.
The court ​has a 6-3 conservative majority. Liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated they would have denied the request.
The FCC, which currently has a 2-1 Republican majority, modified its so-called "lowest unit charge" rule in March in a move seen as a boost to President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans. The president's party is seeking to retain control of Congress in the November 3 midterms.
"We are pleased the Supreme Court has granted the FCC's stay request. The court's decision is right on the law and avoids the specter of upending ‌the rules for political ads right in the middle of ⁠an ongoing election," an FCC spokesperson said.
Chief Justice John Roberts had previously lifted the October 9 deadline that was given to the FCC by the Richmond-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals. The 4th Circuit has accused the FCC of repeated "delay tactics" in ⁠the case, and emphasized the need for an urgent ruling in the Democratic challenge given the looming election.
The Supreme Court's latest action marks the second time in recent weeks that it has addressed the FCC's policy, as major Republican committees head toward the midterms with a cash advantage over their Democratic counterparts.
In September, the court granted a request by the national Republican ​committees ​that support the party's candidates in Senate and House of Representatives races to revive the policy ​after the 4th Circuit blocked it. The justices in an ‌8-1 ruling said that the Democratic candidates must wait for the FCC to rule before filing a challenge in court.
The FCC policy at issue requires broadcasters to charge discounted rates for airing certain political advertisements within 60 days of a general election, a window that opened this year on September 4.
A group of Democratic candidates including Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia in April challenged the policy through in-house proceedings at the FCC. When the agency took no action, the Democrats successfully challenged the policy in the 4th Circuit, a ruling that was later halted by the Supreme Court.
The 4th Circuit on October 7 ordered the FCC to issue a prompt ruling on the ‌Democratic in-house challenge, more than five months after it was filed. In its 2-1 ruling, the ​4th Circuit said its "willingness to tolerate the FCC's delay tactics is at an end."
The Republican committees ​in their Supreme Court filing accused the 4th Circuit of having "short-circuited" the ​FCC's review process.
The Democratic candidates, for their part, accused the FCC in court papers of engaging in "blatant procedural trench warfare to stave ‌off judicial review of an unlawful agency directive until it is ​too late to matter."
The FCC policy gained ​greater significance after the Supreme Court in June struck down federal restrictions on spending coordinated between parties and their candidates, siding with Republican challengers including Vice President JD Vance. Since the June ruling, Republican committees have blown past the former limits ahead of the midterms.
The two Republican committees have exceeded the ​former national caps by more than $48 million, according to Federal ‌Election Commission spending disclosures for July and August. Their Democratic counterparts also eclipsed the former limits, but by much less — just under $4 million.
The three ​main national Republican committees ended August with about $233 million in cash. Their Democratic counterparts held roughly $130 million but also carried nearly $18 million in ​debt, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
(Reporting by John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham)

articles.title_orig: Civic Media Expands With Acquisitions in Iowa and Illinois
articles.title_zh: Civic Media Expands With Acquisitions in Iowa and Illinois
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Business and Law
Wisconsin-based Civic Media Inc. plans to acquire 13 radio stations and several translators in southeast Iowa and west central Illinois from the Pritchard family.
Civic Media currently owns stations in Wisconsin, Michigan, and Minnesota.
The sale, which needs FCC approval, involves stations owned by Pritchard Broadcasting Corp., Titan Broadcasting LLC and Galesburg Broadcasting Co.
Kalil & Co. served as broker for the transaction. The sale price was not disclosed.
“These stations have earned an important place in their communities through relationships they have built with listeners, local businesses and community organizations. We recognize the value of those local connections and look forward to building on that foundation as we expand our presence into these markets,” said Sage Weil, CEO and founder of Civic Media in the announcement.
Titan Broadcasting has been owned by John C. “LJ” Pritchard since 2007, according to a press release. Pritchard Broadcasting Corp. and Galesburg Broadcasting were owned and operated by John T. Pritchard until his death in August.
John C. Pritchard was quoted in the announcement, “Like my father, I believe strongly that small towns need their own media outlets to help disseminate important local information, support a vibrant business community and keep the local public informed about hyper-local matters.
“Joining the Civic Media family provides the best path forward for these stations to continue to serve the local communities today and grow and flourish long into the future,” he said.
Civic Media will acquire KGRS(FM), KBKB(AM/FM), KBUR(AM), KKMI(FM), KDMG(FM), KHDK(FM) and WQKQ(FM), in the Burlington, Iowa, market.
Also coming to Civic Media will be WLSR(FM) WGIL(AM), WKAY(FM), WAAG(FM) and WZIE(FM) in Galesburg, Ill.
Civic Media said listeners can continue to look to the stations for familiar programming.
“Across our footprint, we are committed to covering the stories most relevant to the markets we serve,” Weil said in the media release.
“We believe radio plays a crucial role in our local communities and we look forward to supporting the teams at Titan Broadcasting, Pritchard Broadcasting, and Galesburg Broadcasting Company in fulfilling that role.”
Civic Media was founded in 2022. The company calls itself a “public benefit corporation” dedicated to providing quality broadcast and digital hometown radio focusing on local, regional and state issues.

articles.content_orig:

Join Chrome Unboxed Plus for just $2 a month to get an ad-free experience, access to our private Discord, and more. Learn more about membership here. Ever since Google officially launched the new Googlebook platform, one of the biggest questions hanging in the air has been what this means for existing Chromebook hardware. While we wait for official transition paths for existing Chromebook hardware, the enthusiast community isn’t sitting on its hands.
Over on the r/Googlebook subreddit , user u/mawitime shared photos and impressions after successfully booting a “Frankensteined” version of Googlebook OS onto an existing ASUS Chromebook Plus. And while getting an experimental OS to boot on unsupported hardware is a neat party trick on its own, the real headline is how well it actually runs.
One of the lingering concerns with Googlebook OS being built on a heavier Android foundation is whether it will bog down older or more modest laptop processors. According to u/mawitime, the exact opposite is true.
Running on an ASUS Chromebook Plus equipped with an Intel Core i5-1235U processor, 16GB of LPDDR5 RAM, and 256GB of UFS 3.1 storage (that’s no slouch), the user noted that the most shocking takeaway was the sheer speed and fluidity of the operating system.
“Easily the most shocking thing is how fast and smooth it is. This is not going to slow down existing machines at all – in some cases it feels even faster than ChromeOS.”
The poster also added in the comments that while their specific machine had 16GB of RAM, the lightweight feel of the system left them confident it would run just fine on standard 8GB configurations as well .
How did they actually pull this off? Ironically, they used Google’s own agentic AI tools to make it all work.
In the thread, u/mawitime explained that they spent several days working alongside Google Antigravity to piece together a bootable build, likely pulling from an official ASUS Googlebook recovery image. Because this was a rough build, plenty of hardware drivers weren’t cooperating out of the gate – leaving essentials like Wi-Fi, audio, and Pixel cross-device integration broken for the time being.
However, the modding community is already organizing. Much like the famous “Brunch” framework that allowed users to install full ChromeOS on standard Windows PCs for years, developers are already tinkering with a new repository called gbrunch aimed at bringing Googlebook OS to unofficial x86 hardware .
While we obviously don’t recommend wiping your daily driver Chromebook to install a driver-less build of Googlebook OS today, seeing it fly on a 12th-Gen Intel processor is fantastic news. It proves that Google’s new desktop architecture isn’t just reserved for bleeding-edge silicon and it has the optimization legs to make existing hardware feel brand new.  Stay tuned!

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania doctors are seeing what measles can do to previously healthy, unvaccinated kids
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania doctors are seeing what measles can do to previously healthy, unvaccinated kids
articles.content_orig:
Latest fatality is unvaccinated woman, 39, with ‘underlying conditions’ but CDC still lists only two deaths nationwide
A sixth death has been announced in Pennsylvania ’s measles outbreak, as new figures show cases in the state have risen above 1,100.
The most recent fatality was reported in Franklin county on Monday in a statement posted to Facebook by its coroner. The victim was identified as a 39-year-old female who “had several underlying conditions, including a past diagnosis of measles with treatment”.
The coroner, James Conner, said it was the first measles-related death in the county “for many years” – and that the patient’s recent diagnosis met the definition of the Pennsylvania health department for inclusion.
Five other people have died after contracting measles since August in Pennsylvania, which state officials said on Monday had now recorded 1,137 cases and 219 hospitalizations. The outbreak began west of Philadelphia in April, with authorities blaming low vaccination rates.
The federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), however, continues to list deaths nationally at two amid a dispute between the Trump administration’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy, and Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, over the methodology for classifying measles-related fatalities.
The CDC’s website , last updated on Friday, shows 4,080 confirmed measles infections across the US in 42 separate outbreaks, the highest figures in decades, and almost double the number of cases for the whole of 2025.
Earlier in October, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, declared an emergency because of rising case numbers in her state; while Ohio, South Carolina, Texas and Utah have also seen significant increases.
A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania health department told NBC News on Monday that it was aware of the Franklin county fatality – and was “conducting a thorough review of the reported death”.
The coroner’s office told the outlet through a spokesperson that the woman’s “primary cause of death was a probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles”. The coroner’s office spokesperson said the woman was not vaccinated.
Conner’s statement did not identify the woman to protect the privacy of the victim and relatives. “Families deserve the dignity to mourn in private,” that statement said.
“We strongly encourage our medical community, first responders, and the public to follow the precautions set forth by” Pennsylvania state guidelines.
Those state guidelines recommend two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine, or a combined MMRV vaccine including varicella (chickenpox) protection for children 12 and older.
The CDC website recommends the same vaccinations, but Kennedy – a longtime vaccine skeptic – has offered mixed messages. In March 2025, he questioned the effectiveness of the measles vaccine, saying people should be able “to make that choice for themselves ” about whether to take it.
And in September, he told anti-vaccine activists at a conference in Washington DC that they had “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House”, a month after telling US families in response to the rise in measles cases nationwide that parents “ should get their children vaccinated ”.
The Pennsylvania outbreak has seen 157 new cases over the last week, state figures showed, and one-third of the overall number of infections have come in those 18 or under. Fewer than 1% of cases occurred in those who are fully vaccinated.
The first two fatalities, reported in August, were infants, one whose mother had measles during her pregnancy, and the second a six-week-old who also had a rare genetic condition.
The other Pennsylvania victims were women aged 40 and 20, and an 18-year-old, all of whom had coexisting health conditions.

articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk has suggested that the US government may be behind restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to SpaceX's Starlink internet network.
Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said unexpected new speed limits were disrupting its battlefield missions.
An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky said he believed the restrictions were not a coincidence and were related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington.
Musk said that Starshield, the military-grade sister service to Starlink, is controlled by the US government, and "any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".
Musk - writing on X - had been responding to pleas from Ukrainian officials to restore connectivity, including from Zelensky who told UK media: "I hope that it's a mistake, maybe [a] huge technical problem. I don't know, but we are asking to... switch [it] on."
Starlink, which is owned by Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
It had been partially restored by Wednesday evening, Ukraine's former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said.
"Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense," he wrote on X, thanking Elon Musk and asking for his "continued support".
About an hour later, Musk replied to that post, defending his company's involvement.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he wrote.
Musk added that Starlink is for "civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".
The US government has not commented.
While both companies are owned by Musk's SpaceX, Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas, while Starshield is designed for government and military use.
The restrictions on Tuesday night came as Russia launched deadly attacks against Ukraine that killed several people in Kyiv, officials said, and hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
President Zelensky said it was "one of the largest attacks" from Russia, and while "a significant part of the drones were shot down" there were "also hits".
At least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity, and residents said they received no warning of incoming drones before they hit.
"It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," Zelensky's adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram on Wednesday morning.
US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated towards Ukraine as it continues to strike Russian energy facilities.
Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire, but on Tuesday, Trump denied this.
Speaking during a visit to London on Wednesday, President Zelensky agreed that he had felt betrayed after the US made a deal with Russia to import 300,000 tonnes of its diesel.
"Really yes... but it's a little bit more complicated than just my emotions or my feelings," Zelensky said, when asked by UK journalist Piers Morgan if he felt betrayed.
During his one-day visit , Zelensky was greeted with a hug by UK PM Andy Burnham at Downing Street and held an audience with King Charles.
Ahead of the president's arrival, No 10 announced it would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Ukraine, which have been used to bring down Russian drones.
"We are behind you and that will not change," Burnham told Zelensky.

articles.title_orig: Justice Dept. demands California prove citizenship for lists of voters or withhold ballots
articles.title_zh: Justice Dept. demands California prove citizenship for lists of voters or withhold ballots
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The U.S. Department of Justice has ratcheted up its pressure campaign on California election officials to ferret out alleged voter fraud ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election, demanding that officials statewide prove the U.S. citizenship of thousands of voters flagged by the federal government as potential noncitizens, or withhold or set aside their ballots.
Acting Deputy Atty. Gen. Trent McCotter made the demand — which experts called highly questionable at a time when votes are already being cast — in letters to state election officials Tuesday, including Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Dean Logan, head of the L.A. County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk’s office.
The letters, reviewed by The Times, call on the state officials to respond to the Justice Department within 48 hours.
McCotter wrote that the Justice Department had provided Logan’s office with a “password-protected thumb drive with a list of names the Federal Government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot” for the Nov. 3 election.
“We request that you review the list within 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are listed. For individuals whom you cannot independently confirm citizenship status, we request that you immediately instruct the appropriate elections officials to segregate — not cancel — those individuals’ vote-by-mail ballots until their citizenship status can be determined,” McCotter wrote to both Weber and Logan.
Voters on the federal list who haven’t already been sent a ballot should not be sent one until their citizenship is verified, while ballots already returned by voters on the list should not be counted until their citizenship is verified, McCotter wrote.
Weber’s office did not respond to a request for comment.
Logan said his office was reviewing the Justice Department letter in coordination with Weber and California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta, but had not accessed the USB drive because state officials “do not consider the device a secure medium” and accessing its contents “would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols.”
He said that maintaining accurate voter records is a fundamental responsibility of his office, but also that federal and state laws “are clear on how voter eligibility is established — and any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”
L.A. County says it has received federal grand jury subpoenas demanding voter registration information on dozens of individuals the Trump administration suspects may not be U.S. citizens.
Weber previously questioned the basis for a claim by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in July that there may be more than 190,000 noncitizen voters on California rolls, and rebuffed Trump administration offers to work with her office to purge state polls of such ineligible voters ahead of November without additional information on how it reached its conclusions.
Similar Trump administration lists have been shown in other states to be substantially inaccurate, and to include many voters who are indeed citizens. Election experts say that makes the demand on California — where ballots have already been mailed out — even more concerning.
“One must question why the DOJ would violate its own rules about investigating elections close to election day, and over a week after they knew the state had already mailed ballots out, particularly when their past claims have been full of errors,” said David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research.
Becker noted the Trump administration alleged that there were nearly 16,000 noncitizens registered in Nevada, later reduced that number to 185 after additional scrutiny, and then determined all of them were in fact citizens.
A Justice Department spokesperson, in a statement to The Times, defended the agency’s demands to California — saying it “should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring.”
The spokesperson said the agency could not provide the exact number of voters whose citizenship is being questioned, but that it is in the thousands.
McCotter wrote that if Weber cannot implement his demands for how to segregate ballots and verify voter citizenship for those on the federal list, the Justice Department “will have no choice but to seek emergency relief” — an apparent reference to seeking court intervention.
McCotter copied on the letters First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the lead federal prosecutor in Los Angeles whose office previously sent Logan’s office a series of grand jury subpoenas for individual voter records as part of a criminal investigation into illegal voting.
Essayli’s office referred questions to the Justice Department. Bonta’s office referred questions to Weber and Logan.
Federal investigators have sent L.A. County election officials multiple grand jury subpoenas as part of a criminal investigation into illegal voting, according to records reviewed by The Times.
Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA School of Law, said that he is “not aware of anything like this ever happening this close to an election,” and that it may in fact be illegal under the National Voter Registration Act, which “prevents systematic purges of voters 90 days before the election.”
He said that the question of whether that preclusion against purges applies to the removal of noncitizens is an issue that is currently before the U.S. Supreme Court , in an Arizona case the high court will hear in December, but that the Justice Department’s actions strike him as “legally questionable.”
Hasen said the “whole point of that 90-day rule is to prevent the inadvertent disenfranchisement of eligible voters by mistake in the rush before the election,” and that risk is increased by the inaccuracies of similar lists presented by the Trump administration in other states. “So if there is an attempt to go to court — if DOJ tries to sue over this — they might have a hard time getting a judge to agree that this is something that the registrar must do or even can do.”
The fact that election officials are already busy receiving and preprocessing ballots would only bolster the state’s position in such a case, Hasen said.
Across California and the nation, Democratic leaders and voting rights advocates are ramping up coordination and gaming out responses to a raft of potential actions by the Trump administration to subvert the November vote or deny its outcome.
“It’s obviously not a convenient time,” he said. “And given the fact that the lists have proven to be wildly inaccurate, at least in other states, it might be sending the registrar on a wild goose chase, when they have more relevant things to do in the election.”
But that “chaos” may be the point, Hasen said. “This is potentially another example of DOJ just making the work of state and local election administrators — which is already quite difficult and stressful — even harder,” he said.
Attorneys with the UCLA Voting Rights Project filed a lawsuit last month on behalf of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA, and a California voter named Pedro Trujillo, in which they challenged the Trump administration’s use of unproven federal databases to allege registered California voters are not citizens.
On Wednesday, they told the Justice Department that they would be seeking emergency relief from such practices, given McCotter’s letters.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo slept well after cancer surgery, but recovery could take ‘longer than expected’
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo slept well after cancer surgery, but recovery could take ‘longer than expected’
articles.content_orig:
VATICAN CITY — Pope Leo XIV’s recovery from lung surgery could take “longer than expected,” the president of Peru warned Wednesday, as the leader of the Roman Catholic Church continued to mend at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital.
Keiko Fujimori, in an interview on Peruvian television, said the pace of the pope’s recovery could determine whether Leo makes his weeklong apostolic visit to Peru, which was set to start Nov. 11.
“I want the pope to know that here in Peru, millions of us are praying for his speedy recovery,” Fujimori said. “We will also be watching for any announcements from the Vatican, because we understand that his recovery will take several weeks longer than expected and, therefore, we also understand that there could be some changes to the schedule of his visit.”
Leo, who is a Chicago native , spent more than two decades working in Peru and maintains close ties with that South American country.
Fujimori’s announcement was somewhat at odds with the Vatican’s assertion on Wednesday that the pope was recovering as expected after an operation to remove part of his right lung, which confirmed a cancer diagnosis .
The medical team taking care of the 71-year-old said he had undergone routine blood tests and a chest X-ray and that, so far, the results “confirm a normal post-operative course: the values are within the expected range for the type of procedure performed.”
The pope has begun walking around his hospital room and ate both breakfast and lunch on Wednesday, they said.
So far, Leo’s doctors have given no indication that the pontiff might need any further treatment. And the Vatican has not indicated whether the cancer might have spread.
In the meantime, the Vatican released its first post-surgery message from the pope, which was addressed to the participants at a meeting to mark the 10th anniversary of “Amoris Laetitia,” a 2016 document on Catholic doctrine released by Pope Francis.
“As you know, I have been unable to be among you during these days,” the message stated. “I thank you warmly for your prayers and for the work you have done together. Your sharing of experiences and attentive listening are indeed a gift to the whole Church.”
As the pontiff continues with recovery, his brother, Louis Prevost, is being treated for blood cancer, a source close to the Prevost family told NBC Chicago .
In an interview with Newsmax’s Rob Finnerty , Prevost said they’re optimistic the pope will rally.
“They caught it early enough, and he’ll be able to heal from the surgery and go on with his papal ministry,” he said.
Leo was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, a type of non-small cell lung cancer, after doctors examined the nodule they had removed from his right lung.
Non-small cell lung cancer accounts for 80% of all cases of the disease, according to the American Lung Association.
Leo spent a calm night in the hospital after surgery to remove a malignant lung nodule was completed “successfully, on schedule and as planned,” the Vatican said Tuesday. Leo was in the operating room for nearly three hours, it said.
The initial lump was detected during a routine check, the Vatican has said. The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics took the rare step of revealing the health issue — the first of his papacy — during his Sunday noon prayer.
Leo waved to crowds outside Rome’s Gemelli Hospital as he entered Tuesday.
The procedure was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, with medical staff reciting the rosary prayer in the hospital chapel as the operation began.
Following his surgery, the pontiff “woke up normally and, after a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the tenth floor,” the Vatican said. The room is next to the usual papal apartment, complete with private chapel, which is currently undergoing renovations.
This type of cancer affects both smokers and nonsmokers, although Leo is not known to ever have been a smoker.
The cancer diagnosis could complicate his busy schedule.
Just weeks earlier, hundreds of thousands of people packed the streets of Paris for an outdoor Mass on a visit that saw Leo warn about the risks of artificial intelligence.
He was planning to take a historic two-week visit to South America next month, although it is unclear if that will still go ahead.
Messages of support and sympathy flowed in after the news.
Dr. Fernando Daniels III, a 67-year-old physician from Maryland, was among many praying for Leo’s swift recovery in the Vatican’s St. Peter’s Square.
“I’ve seen miracles in medicine. I’ve seen people told with terminal illnesses they wouldn’t live and they did,” he told NBC News.
“Prayers of all should heal him,” said Daniels, who was traveling as part of a group.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he and his wife, Jeanette Rubio, were praying for the pope.
“May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” Rubio said on X.
“We thank God that the surgery on Pope Leo was, by all accounts, successful, and that he continues his recovery and recuperation,” New York City’s Archbishop Ronald Hicks said in a statement.
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, whose role is largely ceremonial, wished Leo a speedy and full recovery, the German Catholic news agency KNA reported.
“The pope’s voice on the current issues and challenges of our time is of particular importance and of value to many people worldwide, including in Germany, beyond denominational boundaries,” Steinmeier was quoted as saying.
Claudio Lavanga reported from Vatican City, Mithil Aggarwal from Hong Kong and Corky Siemaszko from New York City.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.
Mithil Aggarwal is a Hong Kong-based reporter/producer for NBC News.
Corky Siemaszko is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Burnham treads carefully in Zelensky visit, balancing Trump and Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Burnham treads carefully in Zelensky visit, balancing Trump and Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
President Volodymyr Zelensky's visit to London follows a well-trodden diplomatic path in a war now in its fifth year.
For months, US President Donald Trump had been a largely benign presence in the conflict, promising Ukraine greater access to American air defence technology and threatening more sanctions on Russia.
Then last week Trump carried out an abrupt U-turn, lifting sanctions on Russian diesel and calling for Zelensky to be replaced.
Once again Ukraine's leader got on his plane to shore up support among European allies. Today London, tomorrow Brussels.
For the prime minister there was the tricky but now familiar diplomatic task of needing to show solidarity with Zelensky without appearing to criticise Trump.
Burnham's answer was to say and announce as much as he could without exposing himself to questions from journalists asking about Trump's latest betrayal of Kyiv.
So Downing Street issued an embargoed press notice overnight with warm words of support for Zelensky.
It said Burnham would promise to go "further and faster" in helping Ukraine with financial and military aid.
Specifically, the prime minister would pledge to speed up the delivery of lightweight multirole missiles that can help bring down fast jet-powered Russian drones.
There was a military honour guard in Downing Street to greet Ukraine's president, followed by a controlled photo opportunity showing the start of the meeting between the two men.
In No 10, before that meeting, Burnham told Zelensky that Britain stood with him "at this difficult time".
He said it was clear "who the aggressor is" after Russia's attacks on Ukraine's critical national infrastructure. And crucially he praised Zelensky for his "leadership" in being prepared to sit down and discuss Donald Trump's call for an energy ceasefire.
In his reply, Zelensky said it was an "absolutely terrible time" for Ukraine. There was no energy ceasefire, he said, but Russian escalation instead.
He said Ukraine "counted on partnership with the US" but spoke of "some difficulties" and "different surprises" with Ukraine's access to US intelligence and the Starlink satellite network.
Following the meeting, Downing Street said the two men had emphasised how Russia had launched "blatant indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure" after President Trump's call for an energy ceasefire. It was clear, they agreed, "Russia had no interest in peace".
They also discussed how the UK could speed up defensive support for Ukraine ahead of the winter - as well as "retrofitting British capability" on military equipment provided by other allies.
In the House of Commons, at the start of his weekly question time, Burnham used the opportunity to offer what he called his "unwavering" support for Zelensky and promise greater military and financial aid in the future.
But it fell to the Liberal Democrat leader, Sir Ed Davey, to ask the question journalists might have asked if they had the chance.
Sir Ed said the prime minister had studiously avoided commenting on Trump's decision to rip up international sanctions on Russia.
"This House does deserve to know his position, as does frankly President Zelensky and our brave Ukrainian allies," Sir Ed said.
"Doesn't he agree this is yet another shameful Trump betrayal of the Ukrainian people and European security?"
In reply, Burnham admitted it was a "very dark and difficult moment" for Zelensky, who was "carrying the heaviest of weights" right now.
But Burnham eschewed the chance to criticise Trump and told MPs this: "What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back and therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together."
"That is the role I intend to play - it's the right role for me to play - in this moment. I will listen to President Zelensky carefully but he won't be going away from Britain today empty handed."
In other words, do not expect the prime minister to join in the widespread European criticism of Trump.
After the now infamous falling out between Trump and Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025 , the UK played a key role in calming the row and bringing both sides back together.
A key player was national security adviser Jonathan Powell, who shuttled between Washington and Kyiv pouring oil on troubled waters. It seems Burnham hopes the UK can play a similar bridge-building role now.
For millions of Ukrainians facing a grim winter potentially with less US support than before, the task could not be more urgent.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive: Judge limited Justice Department access to Rep. Ilhan Omar’s records in sprawling immigration fraud probe
articles.title_zh: Exclusive: Judge limited Justice Department access to Rep. Ilhan Omar’s records in sprawling immigration fraud probe
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration pushed for an unusually aggressive search of Rep. Ilhan Omar ’s house in recent days in an immigration fraud probe that targets the congresswoman, possible false statements made on government documents, and a potential conspiracy, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation.
Prosecutors, however, first had to contend with a federal magistrate judge, in a prolonged back-and-forth that hasn’t previously been reported. Judge Matthew Sharbaugh of the DC District Court ultimately limited how the Justice Department could access Omar’s documents in Monday’s search, before he would approve the warrant, because of her role as a member of Congress and the Constitutional protections that affords, multiple people familiar with the investigation told CNN.
The investigators’ inquiries that prompted the search include whether Omar or her now-deceased father lied about her age when she obtained citizenship in 2000, claiming she was a minor when she was of adult age.
Omar emigrated to the US as a Somalian refugee around the age of 12 and became a citizen in 2000, according to people familiar with Omar’s situation.
One source told CNN the government could try to expand the investigation into a wider conspiracy case and try to investigate if this was deception and the purposeful falsification of information over years by a larger group of individuals.
Federal agents raid Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home two days after President Trump lashed out at her on stage
Omar has been under criminal investigations for years — including before Trump took office last year. But the Trump administration has pushed further with the belief that she has repeated false statements when filling out government documents, such as a passport, in recent years. That is what led to the search on Monday, the sources say.
The search of her home in DC was highly unusual for its timing less than a month before Election Day voting ends, including while Omar is running for reelection as a Democrat in Minnesota.
The effort is also the federal push this month has also been unusual for its attempt to access a member of Congress’ records — the type of criminal investigative work that Republicans this year have made into a political firestorm for past administrations.
As part of the renewed probe, at least a dozen subpoenas were issued beginning last Friday to witnesses, most of them relatives, according to people familiar with the investigation.
Government records and archives in Somalia are notoriously unreliable and hard to access due to years of conflict and disconnected government entities.
In recent weeks, the Justice Department argued for broad access to records that Omar kept at her home in Washington, the sources said.
The Justice Department has argued that with Omar there was little need for sequestering the records taken from her home on Monday.
But the judge who ultimately approved the search told the Justice Department that wasn’t possible under the law, the sources said. Sharbaugh of the DC District Court told prosecutors from DC they would need to set up a process for screening the records to protect Omar’s legislative work from investigators.
In DC, the courts have upheld expansive protections around records of legislative work for members of Congress under the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause.
The multi-day back-and-forth between the judge and the Justice Department in recent days hasn’t been previously reported.
It may now have vast implications for both federal investigators that are looking to potentially charge Omar with a crime and for her campaign.
The Justice Department’s approach to the search also was especially notable because Omar, a US citizen originally from Somalia, is a high-profile member of the group of female progressives known as “The Squad,” a top and frequent political target of President Donald Trump and is running for re-election to Congress in Minnesota, where voting in the mid-term elections has already begun.
Omar has publicly called the search of her home a political attack prompted by the hatred that Trump and Republicans have for her.
“This is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar said in a post on social media on Monday. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.”
She has denied any wrongdoing and hasn’t been charged with a crime. An attorney for Omar didn’t respond to multiple requests for this story.
Investigators are looking into an unsubstantiated claim around whether her now ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, was her brother, in order to get him citizenship — a claim that has been repeated by Trump and which Omar has called “bigoted lies.”
Even if substantiated, the statute of limitations would have long run out over any crime, and it’s unclear what role that would play in the inquiry, informed sources told CNN.
No charges were brought by the Biden-era investigators and the case around Omar didn’t progress nearly as far as the current Trump-era investigators have taken it, several people familiar with the investigation said.
The case was reopened last year and is now being led by prosecutors in the deputy attorney general’s office and in the US attorney’s office in Minneapolis, the sources said. The US Attorney’s Office in Washington, DC, has also been involved.
Any new case, if charged, would likely be complicated by Trump’s rhetoric against Omar, over many years and some of it being racist. Vice President JD Vance has also talked about discussing the case with White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, and White House border czar Tom Homan has repeatedly talked on Fox News about an ongoing investigation into Omar.
“If someone committed immigration violation, someone committed marriage fraud or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law, so I’ll leave it at that,” Homan said in a September interview after mentioning an “ongoing criminal investigation” around Omar.
A separate investigation of possible financial misconduct, including around campaign finance, also continues in the DC US attorney’s office.
DC US Attorney Jeanine Pirro was asked on Tuesday on Fox News about Omar’s financial disclosures that House ethics investigators previously scrutinized.
“That is the subject of an investigation as well,” Pirro said. “We’re looking at the facts. Based upon the facts we will follow them wherever they take us.”
Since the DC federal court’s oversight of the search of Omar’s home, any criminal investigation that would rely on her own records may be slowed down substantially, and has already raised concerns about Justice Department integrity and politicization.
Judges in the DC District Court have grown increasingly skeptical of the Trump administration’s approach to Constitutional protections in criminal cases, especially when those cases appear politically charged.
At the same time, Republicans have been furious with the Justice Department under President Joe Biden for seeking Congress members’ communications in past criminal investigations. Republicans on Capitol Hill and Trump have been particularly critical of former special counsel Jack Smith obtaining secrecy orders when Smith’s office subpoenaed phone companies for call logs of members around the January 6, 2021, US Capitol attack conspiracy investigation.
Generally, the Justice Department avoids overt investigative activity that could affect an election within 60 days of Election Day.
In this case, however, top Justice officials signed off on Monday’s HSI search.

articles.title_orig: Your flu shot can’t wait
articles.title_zh: Your flu shot can’t wait
articles.content_orig:
When news breaks, you need to understand what actually matters — and what to do about it. At Vox, our mission to help you make sense of the world has never been more vital. But we can’t do it on our own.
We rely on readers like you to fund our journalism. Will you support our work and become a Vox Member today?
Some parts of the country are already seeing case levels typical of late fall or early winter.
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .
Flu season is starting earlier than usual this year, which I know from reviewing federal data. But I also know it because I woke up with body aches and chills last night, mere days before I’d planned to get my flu vaccination (!).
Already, some parts of the country are seeing levels of flu activity typically associated with late fall or early winter. In Washington state, for instance, doctors are reporting seeing as much flu now as they usually would around Christmas.
Flu activity overall is still low , to be clear. But as of October 7, infections were rising in all 50 states. And flu is spreading before many people — like, say, me — have received their annual vaccine.
Epidemiologists don’t yet know why the flu arrived early this year, or why cases first started rising in Western states like Washington, California, and Nevada. It’s possible that a mutation is helping this year’s flu variants evade existing immunity, one virologist told NPR . International travel could play a role , too: Flu cases also spiked early in Japan and other parts of Asia.
We don’t need to know why the flu arrived early to take some basic precautions, though. So today, we’re talking through some practical tips for coping with an early flu season.
An early flu season doesn’t necessarily mean a worse season — but even a moderate season can do serious damage. Last year, influenza sent hundreds of thousands of people to the hospital and caused tens of thousands of deaths, including almost 200 among children .
The first and best way to avoid those kinds of harms is by getting the flu shot, which reduces the risk of serious illness by an average of 40 to 60 percent. In the US, people aged 6 months and older are typically told to get the vaccine by October’s end.
In light of the early onset, however (it takes two weeks to build up full immunity), you might instead want to get your shot ASAP.
There are some everyday precautions you can take, too — many of them familiar from the Covid-19 era. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and warm water, for slightly longer than feels appropriate. Mask when you’re sick or might encounter someone else who is.
And don’t neglect the good habits that support your overall health: getting enough sleep, drinking a lot of water, and eating a balanced diet. (There’s very little evidence for trendier interventions, like supplements, saunas, cold plunges, or the infused herbal baths that my kooky former yoga teacher used to recommend.)
If you do get flu symptoms, reach out to your doctor early — especially if you’re older, pregnant, immunocompromised, or otherwise at higher risk for complications. Prescription antiviral medications, like Tamiflu, prevent the flu virus from spreading inside your body so that your immune system can clear it. But they work best within 48 hours of symptom onset.
To be clear, you needn’t take my word on any of this; I’m just another voice in the public health cacophony! Besides, recent polling suggests that my particular voice — that is, the voice of someone who works in media — is not quite as persuasive as it used to be. (Ditto medical websites and government health agencies.)
But if you have doubts or questions about vaccines, there is someone much closer to home you can consult : Ask your doctor (or nurse or pharmacist) about the flu shot’s risks and benefits. They’re best positioned to break the science down and apply it to your health. In hindsight, mine surely would have told me to stop delaying my shot for a more convenient weekend.
➨ Get creative in the fight against inflation. The latest inflation numbers are out today, and they are pretty bad . The cost of many goods and services is rising more quickly than both consumers’ incomes and economists’ expectations. For me, this news brought to mind a question that Vox’s former personal finance columnist tackled a few years ago: Namely, am I cursed to keep spending more money on more things forever?! Her answer was essentially “yes,” but she offered a few ways to help offset those costs: things like moving to a cheaper area or pooling resources via initiatives like tool libraries and community gardens.

articles.title_orig: Climate change pushed Earth to its limits in 2026 as certain "vital signs" reach record extremes, report says
articles.title_zh: Climate change pushed Earth to its limits in 2026 as certain "vital signs" reach record extremes, report says
articles.content_orig:
Climate change pushed the Earth's environmental system to, and perhaps beyond, its limits in 2026, as several of its "vital signs" reached record extremes, researchers said in a new report on the state of the global climate.
Of the 16 climate markers that researchers consider integral measures of how the Earth is doing, seven are currently at record extremes, while multiple others show evidence of accelerating or abruptly shifting, the report published Wednesday in the peer-reviewed journal BioScience said.
The markers include greenhouse gases, temperature, glacier mass, oceans, wildfires and the planet's energy imbalance, which refers to the difference between the amount of energy the Earth absorbs and the amount it radiates back out into the atmosphere.
Researchers warned in the report that the planet's climate "is moving deeper into uncharted territory."
"Earth's life-support systems are being pushed beyond stable limits, with changes unfolding faster than our ability to respond," the report said. "Across the globe, extreme heat, floods, droughts, storms, and wildfires are no longer rare events but defining features of a changing planet."
July 2026 broke records as the warmest month ever for the contiguous United States, while the country as a whole was experiencing what turned out to be the hottest summer it had ever seen.
Globally, ocean temperatures also reached new heights in July, the report said, while data show that carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere are higher now than at any other time in the last 2 million years. Heat waves scorched Europe , killing an estimated 14,000, and baked portions of the U.S., too, fueling wildfires that burned millions of acres of land.
Climate change appears to be accelerating, and its effects are becoming more intense, the researchers warned. They noted that the patterns they'd observed while compiling the report had raised concerns about their potential to cross a point of no return, one at which their impacts on various ecosystems would be irreversible.
In 2025, coral reefs became the first environmental system on Earth to reach a climate "tipping point," with researchers saying the damage could be permanent.
Global warming is happening more quickly now than it was a few decades ago, according to the new climate report, which said the rate of warming has sped up, increasing from roughly 0.05 degrees Celsius per decade between 1880 and 1970, to 0.19 degrees Celsius per decade between 1970 and 2010, and 0.36 degrees Celsius per decade between 2010 and 2024.
Faster warming increases the likelihood of crossing tipping points from which different environments can't bounce back, and it also risks destabilizing the delicate balance between them, researchers said.
For example, greenhouse gas emissions from melting permafrost , wildfires, or other natural sources, which are all triggered by the temperatures associated with global warming, could essentially become a cycle that fuels itself.
Amplified sea ice loss, ecosystem degradation and carbon emissions could also begin to create their own self-perpetuating feedback loop — the crux of the "hothouse" climate trajectory, where various tipping points act as catalysts that push global warming far past humans' control.
"We are witnessing the rapid destabilization of the Earth's climate system," the researchers said. "This is no longer a warning for the future; it is a diagnosis of the present."
However, the report noted that worsening trends in fossil fuel combustion and other emissions, the main drivers of the extreme changes it centers on, have been accompanied by positive shifts in renewable energy use.
But the researchers emphasized that any progress seen so far "remains far below the scale and speed needed to stabilize Earth's climate system."
"Rapid reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, effective adaptation, ecosystem protection, and transformative societal change remain essential to reducing climate risks and securing a more resilient and sustainable future," they said.

articles.title_orig: Six projects demonstrate how advanced computing can help solve real-world challenges
articles.title_zh: Six projects demonstrate how advanced computing can help solve real-world challenges
articles.content_orig:
The important challenges shaping our future, including clean energy, public health, climate resilience and natural resource management, are too complex for a single discipline or organization to solve alone. The vision of the Jen-Hsun Huang and Lori Mills Huang Collaborative Innovation Complex is to build a collaborative environment where researchers, students, industry partners and communities can take on those challenges. Enabled by the most advanced NVIDIA supercomputer in higher education, researchers will combine advanced computing and artificial intelligence with the knowledge gained from lived experience and real-world problem solving.
“These projects demonstrate what becomes possible when extraordinary researchers gain access to extraordinary tools,” said Ruben Rathnasingham, executive director of the Huang Complex. “Our goal is not simply to advance computing. It’s to accelerate discoveries that improve lives, strengthen communities and help us better understand the world around us.”
In 2027, six OSU research teams will be among the first projects to run on the supercomputer housed in the Huang Complex on OSU’s Corvallis campus. Their projects will tackle challenges that are urgent, complex and consequential for humanity while helping establish a new model for integrating advanced computing, artificial intelligence and human expertise.
Known as hero runs, the projects are designed to use the supercomputer’s entire power for a single project, in this case using all or most of the new Vera Rubin cluster and available memory. The teams are comprised of researchers from the colleges of Engineering , Science and Earth, Ocean, and Atmospheric Sciences .
Together, the six projects reflect the range of challenges the Huang Complex is designed to address. While each project tackles a different question, they will all use a world-in-the-loop innovation model in which AI is continuously shaped by human expertise, tested in real-world settings and refined through lived experience — ensuring that solutions are designed to earn the trust of the people they serve.
Researchers are developing new approaches to help make nuclear fusion a reliable source of clean energy. By improving our ability to understand and manage complex plasma behavior, this work could help advance a future with abundant, carbon-free energy that supports communities and economies around the world.
Ocean waves shape coastlines, influence ecosystems and affect the safety of coastal communities. This project seeks to improve our understanding of wave behavior, helping researchers develop better tools for managing erosion, preparing for hazards and protecting coastal environments.
This team is studying how light and matter interact at the molecular level, drawing inspiration from natural light-harvesting systems. Their discoveries could support the development of more efficient solar energy technologies and new approaches to sustainable energy generation.
Researchers are developing models that help cities better understand how diseases spread and how communities can respond effectively. The project aims to provide public tools that support healthier, more resilient cities while helping decision-makers prepare for future outbreaks.
Oregon’s forests, watersheds, farms and communities are constantly changing due to fire, floods, development and other forces. This project uses advanced satellite imagery analysis to better understand these changes and support informed decisions about the landscapes that sustain Oregon’s people, economy and ecosystems.
This project will improve our ability to reconstruct and understand weather and climate patterns at unprecedented levels of detail. More accurate climate information can help farmers, water managers, researchers, communities and policymakers make better decisions about the future.
A rigorous review process evaluated the scientific and technical strength of each proposed project and its alignment with OSU’s strategic plan, Prosperity Widely Shared . Each selected project received seed fund grants of up to $75,000 from the Huang Complex Supercomputing Seed Fund , created to financially support research teams seeking to achieve significant scientific, societal, economic and workforce impacts through advanced computing.
OSU’s Research Computing Office is key to creating a research computing ecosystem where projects like the hero runs can benefit from technical support of high-performance computing, accelerated computing and supercomputing, generative and physical AI and more. The office serves as the governance and operational framework designed to maximize the impact of the Huang Complex and OSU’s broader research computing investments.
“The RCO is aligning technology, services and institutional priorities to create a seamless and scalable research environment,” said Ramee Kelly, strategic coordinator with the Office of the CIO. “By coordinating expertise from across the university and fostering collaboration with peer Oregon institutions, state partners, industry collaborators and technology providers, the office ensures that advanced computing capabilities can be leveraged effectively and equitably across disciplines and campuses.”
This coordinated approach reduces barriers for researchers, allowing faculty, students and research teams to focus on solving complex problems rather than navigating fragmented technology ecosystems. The RCO is also focused on building the community needed to fully utilize the capabilities of OSU’s computing investments. Through regular town halls, training opportunities and researcher forums, the office is helping faculty, students and staff develop the skills and readiness required to leverage emerging technologies.
The hero run teams will provide insight into how systems operate, identify any speed bumps and generally pave the way for future users.
“The selection and support of six research teams to conduct the Huang Complex’s inaugural hero runs highlights the extraordinary opportunities GPU-enabled computing creates for advancing discovery across diverse scientific domains,” said Todd Palmer, University Distinguished Professor and senior advisor and chief scientist for OSU’s Research Computing Office. “As early adopters, these teams will provide essential insights into system performance, user workflows and support models, helping to ensure successful onboarding for the broader research community.”

articles.title_orig: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying
articles.title_zh: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying
articles.content_orig:
FSB security agency said reporter was arrested on island of Sakhalin, alleging he was collecting information about Russia’s defences
Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of spying, in the latest sign of rising tensions between Moscow and Tokyo.
Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai, from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, adding that he had been accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.
Japan’s foreign ministry summoned the Russian ambassador in Tokyo, Nikolay Nozdrev, over the arrest later on Wednesday.
Imai, a reporter at the newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin, was reportedly preparing to return to Japan when he was arrested for allegedly collecting information on Russia’s defence capabilities, according to Russia’s Tass news agency.
Russia’s FSB security agency claimed the journalist had intended to pass the information on to Japanese intelligence.
The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.
Japan’s foreign ministry urged Moscow to extend “fair and impartial treatment” to the detained journalist. “The Japanese embassy … in Moscow and the consulate general in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk lodged a request with the Russian authorities for the prompt provision of information, as well as for humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment,” an official told Agence France-Presse.
The Hokkaido Shimbun said in a statement that it was aware of the announcement by Russian authorities but it was “still confirming the details”.
“Ensuring the safety of the journalist is our top priority, and we are responding accordingly,” it said.
Imai’s arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over sovereignty of islands belonging to the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido.
Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war ⁠in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap .
The FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency.
Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.
“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”.
The Kurils have been under Russian control since the end of the second world war, when Soviet forces seized the islands in the final days of the conflict, forcing about 17,000 Japanese citizens to leave and, over time, replacing them with a similar number of Russians.
In 2022, Moscow scrapped a programme that allowed former residents to travel to the islands to visit the graves of their ancestors in protest at Japan’s support for Ukraine.
Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August, causing an ​uproar in Japan . Tokyo has ‌said it would continue ​implementing sanctions against ​Russia and supporting Ukraine.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters
